concepts.name: Scientific method
concepts.statement: Chemistry is a science based on observation and experimentation, and there is no single route from a question to an answer. What every route has in common is that it rests on experiments that can be repeated, so the path from question and observation to hypothesis, and from hypothesis through testing to law or theory, is the method the whole of the book argues by.

concepts.name: Telling a hypothesis, law and theory apart
concepts.statement: Outside science these three words are loose; inside it they are precise. A hypothesis is a tentative explanation that guides the gathering of information, a law summarizes a vast number of observations and predicts, and a theory is a well-substantiated explanation that has survived a large body of data. Knowing which of the three a statement is tells you how much weight it carries.

concepts.name: Domains of chemistry
concepts.statement: Chemists describe matter in three domains at once: the macroscopic, which you can see and touch; the microscopic, which is mostly imagined; and the symbolic, the formulas and equations that stand for either. One challenge of learning chemistry is that the same symbol can stand for a thing in one domain or the other, and one pleasure is explaining what you observe by what you must imagine.

concepts.name: Chemistry
concepts.statement: Chemistry is the study of the composition, properties, and interactions of matter.

concepts.name: Hypothesis
concepts.statement: A hypothesis is a tentative explanation of observations that acts as a guide for gathering and checking information.

concepts.name: Law
concepts.statement: A law is a statement that summarizes a vast number of experimental observations and describes or predicts some aspect of the natural world.

concepts.name: Theory
concepts.statement: A theory is a well-substantiated, comprehensive, testable explanation of a particular aspect of nature.

concepts.name: Macroscopic domain
concepts.statement: The macroscopic domain is the realm of everyday things that are large enough to sense directly by human sight and touch.

concepts.name: Microscopic domain
concepts.statement: The microscopic domain is the realm of things that are much too small to be sensed directly.

concepts.name: Symbolic domain
concepts.statement: The symbolic domain is the specialized language used to represent components of the macroscopic and microscopic domains, such as chemical symbols, chemical formulas, chemical equations, graphs, drawings, and calculations.

concepts.name: Matter
concepts.statement: Matter is anything that occupies space and has mass. A gas is as much matter as a solid is, even though you can neither see nor hold it.

concepts.name: States of matter
concepts.statement: A solid is rigid and keeps its shape, a liquid flows and keeps its volume, and a gas takes both the shape and the volume of its container; a plasma is a gas carrying enough charged particles to behave unlike one. These are the states the book will move a substance between for the rest of the chapters, so the properties that tell them apart come first.

concepts.name: Mass versus weight
concepts.statement: The mass of an object measures the amount of matter in it and does not change; weight is the force gravity exerts on it and changes with the gravity it sits in. An astronaut's mass is the same on the moon as on the earth while her weight is one sixth of it, so it is mass, not weight, that says how much matter is present.

concepts.name: Law of conservation of matter
concepts.statement: There is no detectable change in the total quantity of matter when matter converts from one type to another or changes among the solid, liquid and gaseous states. Every balanced equation and every mass calculation of the later chapters rests on this law, and a mass that seems to vanish has gone somewhere nobody weighed.

concepts.name: Elements and compounds
concepts.statement: A pure substance has a constant composition. An element cannot be broken down into anything simpler by a chemical change; a compound is made of two or more elements and can be broken down into them. The properties of combined elements are nothing like their properties uncombined, which is why sodium and chlorine make table salt.

concepts.name: Homogeneous and heterogeneous mixtures
concepts.statement: A mixture holds two or more kinds of matter in amounts that can vary and can be separated again by physical means. A heterogeneous mixture varies in composition from point to point, as salad dressing does; a homogeneous mixture, also called a solution, is the same throughout, as a sports drink is. The difference is what a sample taken from one place tells about the rest.

concepts.name: Classifying a sample of matter
concepts.statement: Given a sample, you should be able to place it: constant composition or not, uniform or not, simplifiable by a chemical change or not. Two questions sort every sample into an element, a compound, a homogeneous mixture or a heterogeneous mixture, and the classification decides what you can do with the sample.

concepts.name: Atoms and molecules
concepts.statement: An atom is the smallest particle of an element that keeps the properties of that element and can enter into a chemical combination; a molecule is two or more atoms joined by chemical bonds and moving about as a unit. Atoms are far too small and too light to imagine directly, and the whole microscopic domain of the book is built out of them.

concepts.name: Mass
concepts.statement: The mass of an object is a measure of the amount of matter in it, and it does not change with where the object is.

concepts.name: Weight
concepts.statement: The weight of an object is the force that gravity exerts on it, so it changes with the gravity the object is in.

concepts.name: Gas
concepts.statement: A gas is a state of matter that has neither definite volume nor shape.

concepts.name: Liquid
concepts.statement: A liquid is a state of matter that has a definite volume but indefinite shape.

concepts.name: Solid
concepts.statement: A solid is a state of matter that is rigid, has a definite shape, and has a fairly constant volume.

concepts.name: Plasma
concepts.statement: A plasma is a gaseous state of matter containing a large number of electrically charged atoms and/or molecules.

concepts.name: Pure substance
concepts.statement: A pure substance is a homogeneous substance that has a constant composition.

concepts.name: Element
concepts.statement: An element is a substance composed of a single type of atom, one that cannot be decomposed by a chemical change.

concepts.name: Compound
concepts.statement: A compound is a pure substance that can be decomposed into two or more elements.

concepts.name: Mixture
concepts.statement: A mixture is matter that can be separated into its components by physical means.

concepts.name: Heterogeneous mixture
concepts.statement: A heterogeneous mixture is a combination of substances with a composition that varies from point to point.

concepts.name: Homogeneous mixture
concepts.statement: A homogeneous mixture, also called a solution, is a combination of substances with a composition that is uniform throughout.

concepts.name: Atom
concepts.statement: An atom is the smallest particle of an element that can enter into a chemical combination.

concepts.name: Molecule
concepts.statement: A molecule is a bonded collection of two or more atoms of the same or different elements.

concepts.name: Physical properties
concepts.statement: A physical property is a characteristic of matter that is not associated with a change in its chemical composition: density, color, hardness, melting and boiling point, electrical conductivity. Some can be observed without changing the matter at all, and others only while it is changing state, but in neither case does the substance become a different substance.

concepts.name: Chemical properties
concepts.statement: A chemical property is the ability of a substance to change into another kind of matter, or its inability to do so. Flammability, toxicity, acidity and reactivity are chemical properties, and unlike a physical property, one cannot be observed without the substance in question becoming something else.

concepts.name: Physical and chemical change
concepts.statement: A physical change alters the state, form or properties of matter and leaves its chemical identity alone; a chemical change always produces one or more kinds of matter that were not there before. Wax melting and sugar dissolving are the first; rust forming and a match burning are the second, and the test is whether what is left is the same substance.

concepts.name: Classifying a change
concepts.statement: To decide which kind of change a described event is, ask one question: is the matter left afterward the same kind of matter as the matter there before? A gas that expands has changed physically; a gas that has burned has not.

concepts.name: Extensive and intensive properties
concepts.statement: An extensive property depends on how much matter is present and is directly proportional to it; an intensive property does not. Mass and volume are extensive, temperature and density intensive, and the distinction matters because an intensive property identifies a substance while an extensive one only measures a sample of it.

concepts.name: Physical change
concepts.statement: A physical change is a change in the state or properties of matter that does not involve a change in its chemical composition.

concepts.name: Chemical change
concepts.statement: A chemical change is a change producing a different kind of matter from the original kind of matter.

concepts.name: Extensive property
concepts.statement: An extensive property is a property of a substance that depends on the amount of the substance.

concepts.name: Intensive property
concepts.statement: An intensive property is a property of a substance that is independent of the amount of the substance.

concepts.name: Parts of a measurement
concepts.statement: Every measurement provides three kinds of information: a number, a unit that says what the number is compared against, and an uncertainty. You write down the number and the unit and carry the uncertainty implicitly. A quantity missing any of the three is at best confusing: a dose of one hundred without its unit can be a treatment or a lethal amount.

concepts.name: Writing a measurement in scientific notation
concepts.statement: You can write a number in a measurement in decimal form or in scientific notation, and for the very large and the very small only the second is readable. The mass of a mosquito reads better as 2.5 x 10 to the minus 6 kilograms than as a string of zeros, and the notation also settles how many digits of a measurement count.

concepts.name: SI base units
concepts.statement: Seven fundamental properties have units fixed by international agreement, and every other unit in the book is derived from them. Knowing that the meter, the kilogram, the second, the kelvin, the ampere, the mole and the candela are the base units is what makes a unit conversion a matter of bookkeeping rather than of memory.

concepts.name: Using the SI prefixes
concepts.statement: Fractions and multiples of an SI unit are always powers of ten, and each power has a prefix and a symbol. A kilometer is a thousand meters and a microliter is a millionth of a liter, so a reader who knows the prefixes can move a measurement up and down the scale without arithmetic.

concepts.name: Derived units
concepts.statement: Many units are built out of the base units rather than agreed separately: a volume is a length cubed, and a density is a mass divided by a volume. Seeing a unit as the product and quotient of base units lets you check that a calculation has produced the right kind of quantity.

concepts.name: Volume and its units
concepts.statement: Volume is the amount of space an object occupies, and its standard unit is the cubic meter, a cube one meter on an edge. The cubic decimeter is a liter and the cubic centimeter is a milliliter, so the units a chemist actually works in are nested inside the standard one by factors of a thousand.

concepts.name: Density
concepts.statement: The density of a substance is the ratio of the mass of a sample to its volume. It is an intensive property, so it identifies a substance rather than a sample: a brick of gold and a brick of lead of the same size do not have the same mass.

concepts.name: Measuring volume by displacement
concepts.statement: A cube's volume can be calculated from its edge, but most objects are not cubes. Lowering an object into a partly filled graduated cylinder raises the water by exactly the object's volume, which turns an irregular shape into a subtraction and makes the density of anything that sinks measurable with a balance and a cylinder.

concepts.name: Unit
concepts.statement: A unit is a standard of comparison for measurements; the number of a measured quantity says how many of its unit the quantity holds.

concepts.name: Length
concepts.statement: Length is the measure of one dimension of an object, and its SI unit is the meter.

concepts.name: Time
concepts.statement: Time is measured in the SI base unit of time, the second.

concepts.name: Temperature
concepts.statement: Temperature is an intensive property representing the hotness or coldness of matter, and its SI unit is the kelvin.

concepts.name: SI units
concepts.statement: SI units are the standards fixed by international agreement in the International System of Units (Le Système International d’Unités).

concepts.name: Meter
concepts.statement: The meter (m) is the standard metric and SI unit of length; 1 m is approximately 1.094 yards.

concepts.name: Kilogram
concepts.statement: The kilogram (kg) is the standard SI unit of mass.

concepts.name: Second
concepts.statement: The second (s) is the SI unit of time.

concepts.name: Kelvin
concepts.statement: The kelvin (K) is the SI unit of temperature; 273.15 K equals 0 °C.

concepts.name: Degree Celsius
concepts.statement: The degree Celsius (°C) is a unit of temperature; water freezes at 0 °C and boils at 100 °C on this scale.

concepts.name: Cubic meter
concepts.statement: The cubic meter (m³) is the SI unit of volume, the volume of a cube with an edge length of exactly 1 m.

concepts.name: Cubic centimeter
concepts.statement: The cubic centimeter (cm³ or cc) is the volume of a cube with an edge length of exactly 1 cm.

concepts.name: Liter
concepts.statement: The liter (L), also called the cubic decimeter, is a unit of volume; 1 L equals 1,000 cm³.

concepts.name: Milliliter
concepts.statement: The milliliter (mL) is 1/1,000 of a liter and equals 1 cm³.

concepts.name: Exact and uncertain numbers
concepts.statement: Counting is the only measurement free of uncertainty, and numbers fixed by definition are exact in the same way: a foot is exactly twelve inches and an inch exactly 2.54 centimeters. Every other quantity is uncertain to some extent, and knowing which numbers in a calculation are exact decides which of them can limit the answer.

concepts.name: Every measurement carries an uncertainty
concepts.statement: You read a measurement as far as the instrument allows and then one digit further, and that last digit is an estimate. A scale with one milliliter divisions reads to a tenth of a milliliter, and a balance that reads 6.72 grams says the mass lies between 6.71 and 6.73. Uncertainty belongs to the instrument and the person reading it together; it is not a mistake.

concepts.name: Significant figures
concepts.statement: All of the digits in a measurement, including the uncertain last one, are its significant figures, and their number is how a written quantity says how certain it is. A result is properly reported when its significant digits represent the certainty of the process that produced it, and no better.

concepts.name: Counting significant figures
concepts.statement: The rule is to start at the first nonzero digit on the left and count every digit to its right, and the only difficulty is the zeros. A captive zero results from measurement and is always significant, a leading zero only locates the decimal point and never is, and a trailing zero to the left of the decimal point is ambiguous unless the number is written in scientific notation.

concepts.name: Rounding to a given number of digits
concepts.statement: A digit to be dropped that is less than five rounds down, and one greater than five rounds up. When the dropped digit is a five with nothing but zeros after it, round the retained digit to whichever value is even. This rule from statistics keeps the rounding from leaning one way over many calculations.

concepts.name: Carrying significant figures through a calculation
concepts.statement: A result calculated from measurements is at least as uncertain as the measurements it came from, so the answer has to be rounded rather than copied off the calculator. A sum or difference is rounded to the decimal place of the least precise term, and a product or quotient to the number of significant figures of the least certain factor.

concepts.name: Accuracy and precision
concepts.statement: Measurements are precise when repeating them gives very similar results and accurate when they fall close to the true or accepted value, and the two are independent. A dispenser can be precise and consistently wrong, or accurate on average and scattered, and only one that is both is working.

concepts.name: Exact number
concepts.statement: An exact number is a number derived by counting or by definition.

concepts.name: Uncertainty
concepts.statement: The uncertainty of a measurement is an estimate of the amount by which it differs from the true value.

concepts.name: Rounding
concepts.statement: Rounding is the procedure used to ensure that calculated results properly reflect the uncertainty in the measurements used in the calculation.

concepts.name: Accuracy
concepts.statement: Accuracy is how closely a measurement aligns with a correct value.

concepts.name: Precision
concepts.statement: Precision is how closely a measurement matches the same measurement when repeated.

concepts.name: Dimensional analysis
concepts.statement: The units of quantities undergo the same mathematical operations as their numbers. That one premise lets you divide a distance by a time and get a speed. It also lets you check a calculation by looking only at the units, since a wrong arrangement of factors gives a unit nobody wanted.

forms.condition: an average speed, computed from a measured distance and the time taken to cover it

concepts.name: Unit conversion factor
concepts.statement: A ratio of two equivalent quantities in different units equals one, so multiplying by it changes a quantity's units without changing the quantity. The ratio can go either way up, so you choose the arrangement that cancels the unit you want gone and leaves the one you want.

concepts.name: Converting units
concepts.statement: Multiplying by one conversion factor after another, each oriented so that the unwanted unit cancels, converts a measurement through as many steps as it takes. It is the most-used skill of the chapter, and it works the same whether the conversion is between two metric units, between metric and customary units, or between units of an area or a volume.

concepts.name: Computing with mixed units
concepts.statement: Beyond a simple conversion, the factor-label method solves a problem in which the quantity wanted is computed from two or more measured ones given in the wrong units. All the factors are arranged in one line so that the labels cancel and combine into the unit of the answer, and the arithmetic is done once at the end.

concepts.name: Linear versus proportional scales
concepts.statement: Most units of a property are directly proportional to one another and a single conversion factor moves between them. The Celsius and Fahrenheit scales do not share a zero, so the relation between them is a line with an intercept rather than a line through the origin, and converting between them takes both a slope and an offset.

concepts.name: Temperature scales
concepts.statement: You fix a temperature scale by choosing reference temperatures and dividing the space between them. Celsius puts the freezing and boiling of water at 0 and 100, Fahrenheit at 32 and 212. Kelvin is absolute: its zero is the lowest temperature theoretically achievable, and its unit carries no degree symbol.

concepts.name: Converting between Celsius and Fahrenheit
concepts.statement: The Fahrenheit temperature is nine fifths of the Celsius temperature plus thirty-two, and the relation rearranges to give the Celsius temperature from the Fahrenheit one. Both forms are on the book's key equation list, and they are the conversion a reader meets outside the laboratory more often than any other.

concepts.name: Converting between Celsius and kelvin
concepts.statement: A kelvin and a Celsius degree are the same size, so the two scales differ only by where their zeros sit: adding 273.15 to a Celsius temperature gives the kelvin temperature and subtracting it goes back. The 273.15 was determined experimentally and is not exact, which matters when the result is rounded.

concepts.name: Degree Fahrenheit
concepts.statement: The degree Fahrenheit (°F) is a unit of temperature; water freezes at 32 °F and boils at 212 °F on this scale.

concepts.name: Dalton’s atomic theory
concepts.statement: Dalton’s postulates say that matter consists of atoms, and that the atoms of one element all have the same characteristic mass and differ from the atoms of every other element. A compound holds atoms of two or more elements in a small, whole-number ratio. A chemical change neither creates nor destroys atoms but only rearranges them. These postulates explain at the microscopic level the macroscopic behavior of matter you have already met, including the conservation of matter, and every later picture of the atom starts from them.

concepts.name: Law of definite proportions
concepts.statement: All samples of a pure compound contain the same elements in the same proportion by mass, which is what Dalton’s fourth postulate predicts if the numbers of atoms in a compound always stand in the same ratio. Note that the converse is not true: two samples with the same mass ratio are not necessarily the same substance.

concepts.name: Law of multiple proportions
concepts.statement: When two elements form more than one compound, a fixed mass of one element reacts with masses of the other in a ratio of small whole numbers. Taking the ratio of the two mass ratios is the step that reveals it, and atomic theory explains it at once, since one compound simply holds more atoms of one element per atom of the other.

concepts.name: Thomson’s cathode rays and the electron
concepts.statement: The beam in a cathode ray tube bends toward a positive charge and away from a negative one. It is the same whatever metal the electrodes contain, and its charge-to-mass ratio shows that its particles are far lighter than atoms. Thomson concluded that the particles are negatively charged subatomic constituents of all atoms, the first evidence that the atom is not indivisible.

concepts.name: Millikan’s fundamental charge
concepts.statement: The charge on every oil drop Millikan measured is a whole-number multiple of 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, so that value must be the charge of a single electron. Combined with Thomson’s charge-to-mass ratio, it gives the mass of the electron by a simple calculation.

forms.condition: Millikan's charge of the electron divided by Thomson's charge-to-mass ratio

concepts.name: Rutherford’s nuclear atom
concepts.statement: Most α particles pass straight through a gold foil, a few are deflected slightly and a very few bounce almost straight back. Rutherford reasoned that the atom must be mostly empty space with a small, heavy, positively charged nucleus at its center, which replaced both the plum pudding model and the Saturn-like model and is still the picture used today.

concepts.name: Subatomic particles
concepts.statement: An atom is built from three kinds of subatomic particle: the negatively charged, very light electron outside the nucleus, and the positively charged proton and the uncharged neutron of nearly the same mass inside it. Everything the chapter says about atomic number, mass number, isotopes and ions is counted in these three particles.

concepts.name: Isotopes
concepts.statement: Atoms of the same element can differ in mass while remaining chemically identical, because they have the same number of protons and different numbers of neutrons. The existence of isotopes is the reason Dalton’s second postulate had to be restated in terms of chemical properties rather than mass.

concepts.name: Alpha particle
concepts.statement: An alpha particle is a positively charged particle consisting of two protons and two neutrons.

concepts.name: Nucleus
concepts.statement: The nucleus is the massive, positively charged center of an atom, made up of protons and neutrons.

concepts.name: Electron
concepts.statement: An electron is a negatively charged subatomic particle of relatively low mass located outside the nucleus.

concepts.name: Proton
concepts.statement: A proton is a positively charged subatomic particle located in the nucleus.

concepts.name: Neutron
concepts.statement: A neutron is an uncharged subatomic particle located in the nucleus.

concepts.name: Atomic mass unit
concepts.statement: Atoms are so small that grams and coulombs are inconvenient, so their masses are given in atomic mass units, exactly one twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom, and their charges in units of the charge of one electron. On these scales a proton and a neutron each weigh about 1 amu and carry charges of 1+ and 0, and an electron weighs about 0.00055 amu and carries 1−.

concepts.name: Atomic number and mass number
concepts.statement: The atomic number is the number of protons in the nucleus and is the defining trait of an element; the mass number is the total number of protons and neutrons. Their difference is the number of neutrons, and in a neutral atom the atomic number is also the number of electrons.

forms.latex: \begin{array}{rll}\text{atomic number}\;(Z) & = & \text{number of protons} \\ \text{mass number}\;(A) & = & \text{number of protons}+\text{number of neutrons} \\ A-Z & = & \text{number of neutrons}\end{array}

concepts.name: Ions
concepts.statement: When the numbers of protons and electrons in an atom are not equal, it carries a charge equal to the number of protons minus the number of electrons and is called an ion. An atom that gains electrons becomes a negatively charged anion, and one that loses electrons becomes a positively charged cation.

concepts.name: Counting protons, neutrons and electrons
concepts.statement: From an element’s atomic number, a mass number and a charge, you can count the particles. The atomic number gives the protons, the mass number less the atomic number gives the neutrons, and the protons less the charge give the electrons. The same reasoning run backward gives the charge from the counts.

concepts.name: Chemical symbols
concepts.statement: A chemical symbol of one, two or three letters stands for an element or for one atom of it, whether you mean a single atom or a jar full. Only the first letter is a capital, which is why Co is cobalt and CO is carbon monoxide, and some symbols come from the element’s name in another language.

concepts.name: Writing isotope symbols
concepts.statement: The full symbol of an atom places the mass number as a left superscript, the atomic number as a left subscript (often omitted) and the charge as a right superscript on the element’s symbol. Reading and writing these symbols, and the equivalent names such as magnesium-24 or Mg-24, is how the book refers to a particular isotope or ion from here on.

concepts.name: Average atomic mass
concepts.statement: The mass listed for an element in the periodic table is a weighted average over its naturally occurring isotopes, the sum of each isotope’s mass multiplied by its fractional abundance. That is why most atomic masses are not whole numbers, and it is important to understand that no single atom has the average mass: no boron atom weighs 10.8 amu.

forms.condition: a naturally occurring sample of an element, whose isotopes' fractional abundances add up to 1

concepts.name: Finding isotopic abundances
concepts.statement: For an element with two isotopes, the fraction of one can be written as x and of the other as 1 − x, and the average mass equation then becomes one equation in one unknown. Solving it turns the average atomic mass back into the percent composition by isotope.

concepts.name: Mass spectrometry
concepts.statement: A mass spectrometer charges the atoms or molecules of a vaporized sample, deflects the ions through an electric or magnetic field by an amount that depends on their mass and charge, and records how many arrive at each mass-to-charge ratio. The height of each peak is proportional to the fraction of the ions at that ratio, so the spectrum reads off which isotopes are present and in what abundance.

concepts.name: Ion
concepts.statement: An ion is an electrically charged atom or molecule, one that contains unequal numbers of protons and electrons.

concepts.name: Cation
concepts.statement: A cation is a positively charged atom or molecule, one that contains fewer electrons than protons.

concepts.name: Anion
concepts.statement: An anion is a negatively charged atom or molecule, one that contains more electrons than protons.

concepts.name: Atomic number
concepts.statement: The atomic number (Z) of an atom is the number of protons in its nucleus.

concepts.name: Mass number
concepts.statement: The mass number (A) of an atom is the sum of the numbers of neutrons and protons in its nucleus.

concepts.name: Molecular formulas
concepts.statement: A molecular formula writes the symbols of the atoms in a molecule with subscripts giving how many of each there are. Many elements exist as molecules of their own, such as the diatomic H₂, O₂ and N₂ and the eight-atom S₈, and the formula of such an element differs from its symbol for that reason.

concepts.name: A subscript is not a coefficient
concepts.statement: A subscript counts the atoms bonded together in one molecule, while a number written in front counts separate units. H₂ is one molecule of two bonded atoms, 2H is two separate atoms, and 2H₂ is two molecules, four different things for four ways of writing hydrogen.

concepts.name: Structural formulas and molecular models
concepts.statement: A structural formula shows which atoms are connected to which, with lines for bonds; a ball-and-stick model shows the arrangement of the atoms in space, and a space-filling model shows their relative sizes. Each representation adds something the molecular formula leaves out.

concepts.name: Finding an empirical formula
concepts.statement: An empirical formula gives the simplest whole-number ratio of the atoms or ions in a compound, found by dividing the subscripts of the molecular formula by their largest common factor. A molecular formula is always a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula, so acetic acid, C₂H₄O₂, and glucose share the empirical formula CH₂O.

concepts.name: Isomers
concepts.statement: The same atoms can be connected in different ways, so compounds with the same molecular formula can have different structures and different properties. Structural isomers differ in how the atoms are connected, as acetic acid and methyl formate do, and spatial isomers differ only in the orientation of the atoms in space, as the two mirror-image forms of carvone do.

concepts.name: Empirical formula
concepts.statement: An empirical formula shows the composition of a compound as the simplest whole-number ratio of its atoms.

concepts.name: Structural formula
concepts.statement: A structural formula shows the atoms in a molecule and how they are connected.

concepts.name: Structural isomer
concepts.statement: Structural isomers are substances that have the same molecular formula but different physical and chemical properties because their atoms are bonded differently.

concepts.name: Spatial isomers
concepts.statement: Spatial isomers are compounds in which the relative orientations of the atoms in space differ.

concepts.name: Periodic law
concepts.statement: The properties of the elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers. Mendeleev arranged the elements by atomic mass and used the pattern to predict elements not yet found, and by the twentieth century it was clear that atomic number, not mass, orders the table.

concepts.name: Periods and groups
concepts.statement: The modern periodic table arranges the elements in order of increasing atomic number in seven horizontal rows, called periods, and eighteen vertical columns, called groups, so that elements with similar properties fall in the same group. Each box gives the element’s atomic number, symbol and average atomic mass, and a mass in square brackets marks an element made only of radioactive isotopes.

concepts.name: Metals, nonmetals, and metalloids
concepts.statement: Metals are shiny, malleable and ductile and conduct heat and electricity well; nonmetals are dull and conduct poorly; metalloids conduct moderately well and share properties of both. The three classes occupy regions of the periodic table, so an element’s position predicts its general properties.

concepts.name: Main groups and transition metals
concepts.statement: The groups 1, 2 and 13 to 18 hold the main-group elements, groups 3 to 12 the transition metals, and the two rows beneath the table the inner transition metals, the lanthanides and actinides. Several groups have names of their own, the alkali metals, alkaline earth metals, pnictogens, chalcogens, halogens and noble gases, and their members have similar chemical properties.

concepts.name: Naming an element’s group
concepts.statement: Find any element in the periodic table and give the name of its group, and from a group name and a period, find the element. The next two sections rely on this fluency with the table to predict ions and name compounds.

concepts.name: Periodic table
concepts.statement: The periodic table is a table of the elements that places elements with similar chemical properties close together.

concepts.name: Group
concepts.statement: A group is a vertical column of the periodic table.

concepts.name: Period
concepts.statement: A period, also called a series, is a horizontal row of the periodic table.

concepts.name: Metal
concepts.statement: A metal is an element that is shiny, malleable, and a good conductor of heat and electricity.

concepts.name: Nonmetal
concepts.statement: A nonmetal is an element that appears dull and is a poor conductor of heat and electricity.

concepts.name: Metalloid
concepts.statement: A metalloid is an element that conducts heat and electricity moderately well and has some properties of metals and some of nonmetals.

concepts.name: Main-group element
concepts.statement: A main-group element, also called a representative element, is an element in groups 1, 2, and 13–18.

concepts.name: Transition metal
concepts.statement: A transition metal is an element in groups 3–12 (more strictly, 3–11).

concepts.name: Inner transition metal
concepts.statement: An inner transition metal is an element in the bottom two rows of the periodic table; those of the first row are lanthanides and those of the second actinides.

concepts.name: Lanthanide
concepts.statement: A lanthanide is an inner transition metal in the top of the bottom two rows of the periodic table.

concepts.name: Actinide
concepts.statement: An actinide is an inner transition metal in the bottom of the bottom two rows of the periodic table.

concepts.name: Alkali metal
concepts.statement: An alkali metal is an element in group 1.

concepts.name: Alkaline earth metal
concepts.statement: An alkaline earth metal is an element in group 2.

concepts.name: Pnictogen
concepts.statement: A pnictogen is an element in group 15.

concepts.name: Chalcogen
concepts.statement: A chalcogen is an element in group 16.

concepts.name: Halogen
concepts.statement: A halogen is an element in group 17.

concepts.name: Noble gas
concepts.statement: A noble gas, also called an inert gas, is an element in group 18.

concepts.name: Predicting ion charge from the group
concepts.statement: Main-group metals tend to lose enough electrons to have as many as the preceding noble gas and form cations whose charge equals their group number, and nonmetals tend to gain enough electrons to match the next noble gas and form anions whose charge is the number of groups they lie to the left of the noble gases. The rule weakens toward the middle of the table, where metals such as iron and copper form ions of more than one charge.

concepts.name: Polyatomic ions and oxyanions
concepts.statement: A polyatomic ion is a group of bonded atoms that carries an overall charge and acts as a single unit, and an oxyanion is one that contains oxygen. Memorize the names, formulas and charges of the common ones. The suffixes -ate and -ite and prefixes per- and hypo- mark more or fewer oxygen atoms.

concepts.name: Ionic bonds and covalent bonds
concepts.statement: When atoms transfer electrons and form ions, the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions is an ionic bond. When atoms share electrons and form molecules, the attraction between the nuclei and the shared pairs of electrons is a covalent bond. The bonds present in a compound make it ionic or molecular.

concepts.name: Ionic compounds
concepts.statement: A metal combined with one or more nonmetals usually forms an ionic compound, a solid held together by ionic bonds that melts at a high temperature and conducts electricity when molten but not when solid. Its formula gives the relative numbers of ions rather than a molecule, since an ionic compound has no discrete molecules.

concepts.name: Writing ionic formulas
concepts.statement: An ionic compound is electrically neutral, so its formula takes the ions in the ratio that makes the positive and negative charges equal, with a polyatomic ion treated as a unit in parentheses when more than one is needed. Two Al³⁺ and three O²⁻ give Al₂O₃, and one Ca²⁺ with two H₂PO₄⁻ gives Ca(H₂PO₄)₂.

concepts.name: Molecular compounds
concepts.statement: Compounds of nonmetals usually consist of discrete, neutral molecules held together by covalent bonds, and under normal conditions they are often gases, low-boiling liquids or low-melting solids. The book notes that predicting this from positions in the periodic table is a simplistic approach with interesting exceptions.

concepts.name: Predicting ionic or molecular
concepts.statement: Given a formula, find its elements in the periodic table. A metal with nonmetals, or a compound with a polyatomic ion, is ionic, and nonmetals alone form a molecular compound. Ask this question first before you name any compound in the next section.

concepts.name: Monatomic ion
concepts.statement: A monatomic ion is an ion composed of a single atom.

concepts.name: Oxyanion
concepts.statement: An oxyanion is a polyatomic anion composed of a central atom bonded to oxygen atoms.

concepts.name: Covalent bond
concepts.statement: A covalent bond is a bond formed when electrons are shared between atoms.

concepts.name: Ionic bond
concepts.statement: An ionic bond is the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged cations and anions, typically formed when a metal atom transfers electrons to a nonmetal atom.

concepts.name: Naming ionic compounds
concepts.statement: An ionic compound is named cation first and anion second: the metal’s name, then the nonmetal’s name with its ending replaced by -ide, or the name of the polyatomic ion as it stands. Because the charges fix the ratio of the ions, the name does not need to state how many of each there are.

concepts.name: Naming variable-charge metal compounds
concepts.statement: When a metal can form ions of more than one charge, the charge of its ion is worked out from the formula and the anion’s fixed charge and written as a Roman numeral in parentheses after the metal’s name, as in iron(II) chloride and iron(III) chloride. The older suffixes -ous and -ic for the lower and higher charges survive in some industries.

concepts.name: Naming hydrates
concepts.statement: A hydrate is named by adding to the name of the anhydrous compound a Greek prefix for the number of water molecules per formula unit followed by the word hydrate, and its formula appends a centered dot, that number and H₂O. Copper(II) sulfate pentahydrate is CuSO₄·5H₂O.

concepts.name: Naming binary molecular compounds
concepts.statement: Two nonmetals can combine in several ratios, so the name of a binary molecular compound gives the number of each atom with a Greek prefix: the more metallic element first, the other second with the suffix -ide, and mono- dropped from the first. CO is carbon monoxide and N₂O₄ is dinitrogen tetroxide.

concepts.name: Naming binary acids
concepts.statement: A compound of hydrogen and one other nonmetal dissolved in water is named as an acid by turning hydrogen into the prefix hydro-, adding -ic to the other element’s name, and adding the word acid, so that hydrogen chloride in water is hydrochloric acid.

concepts.name: Naming oxyacids
concepts.statement: An oxyacid is named from its oxyanion by omitting hydrogen, replacing -ate with -ic or -ite with -ous, and adding acid, so that H₂CO₃ is carbonic acid and HNO₂ is nitrous acid. Sulfuric and sulfurous acids are the book’s named exceptions.

concepts.name: Hydrate
concepts.statement: A hydrate is a compound containing one or more water molecules bound within its crystals, written with a dot between the formula of the anhydrous compound and the number of water molecules per formula unit.

concepts.name: Nomenclature
concepts.statement: Nomenclature is a system of rules for naming objects of interest, and chemical nomenclature gives every compound a name from which its formula can be written.

concepts.name: Binary compound
concepts.statement: A binary compound is a compound containing two different elements.

concepts.name: Binary acid
concepts.statement: A binary acid is a compound of hydrogen and one other element, bonded so that it releases H⁺ ions when dissolved in water.

concepts.name: Oxyacid
concepts.statement: An oxyacid is a compound of hydrogen, oxygen and one other element, bonded so that it releases H⁺ ions when dissolved in water.

concepts.name: Intermolecular and intramolecular forces
concepts.statement: Intramolecular forces are the bonds within a molecule that keep it together; intermolecular forces are the attractions between molecules, and they decide many of a substance’s physical properties. The intermolecular forces between small molecules are usually weak compared to the bonds within them.

concepts.name: Phase and intermolecular forces
concepts.statement: Intermolecular forces hold particles close together, whereas the particles’ kinetic energy works to separate them, so the phase of a substance depends on the balance between the two. Cooling a gas or compressing it lets the attractions win and it condenses; cooling a liquid far enough lets it freeze.

concepts.name: London dispersion forces
concepts.statement: Because the electrons of an atom or molecule are in constant motion, it can develop an instantaneous dipole, which in turn induces a dipole in a neighbor; the two temporary dipoles attract. This dispersion force is present in all condensed phases, whatever the atoms or molecules.

concepts.name: Polarizability and dispersion forces
concepts.statement: In a larger atom the valence electrons are farther from the nucleus and less tightly held, so the electron cloud is more easily distorted; a more polarizable particle has larger dispersion forces and a higher melting and boiling point.

concepts.name: Molecular shape and dispersion forces
concepts.statement: Molecules with the same formula can have different dispersion forces: an elongated molecule offers more surface area for contact with its neighbors than a compact one, and so it is held more strongly.

concepts.name: Dipole-dipole attractions
concepts.statement: A polar molecule has a partial positive end and a partial negative end, and the positive end of one polar molecule attracts the negative end of another. These attractions add to the dispersion forces, so a polar substance boils higher than a nonpolar one of similar mass.

concepts.name: Hydrogen bonding
concepts.statement: When hydrogen is bonded to fluorine, oxygen or nitrogen, the large difference in electronegativity and the small sizes of the atoms concentrate the partial charges, and the attraction to a similar group in a nearby molecule is a particularly strong dipole-dipole attraction called a hydrogen bond. It is much weaker than a covalent bond but stronger than other intermolecular attractions.

concepts.name: Ranking boiling points
concepts.statement: To compare substances, we identify the forces each can have from its structure: dispersion forces always, dipole-dipole attractions if the molecule is polar, and hydrogen bonding if it has an H–F, H–O or H–N group. With similar sizes, the substance with the stronger forces has the higher boiling point; with the same kind of force, the larger molecule does.

concepts.name: Intermolecular force
concepts.statement: An intermolecular force is a noncovalent attractive force between atoms, molecules or ions. Intermolecular forces are much weaker than the bonds within molecules, yet they decide many physical properties.

concepts.name: Van der Waals force
concepts.statement: A van der Waals force is an attractive or repulsive force between molecules, a name that covers dipole-dipole attractions, dipole-induced dipole attractions and London dispersion forces.

concepts.name: Instantaneous dipole
concepts.statement: An instantaneous dipole is a temporary dipole that exists for a brief moment when the electrons of an atom or molecule happen to be distributed unevenly.

concepts.name: Induced dipole
concepts.statement: An induced dipole is a temporary dipole formed when the electrons of an atom or molecule are distorted by the instantaneous dipole of a neighboring atom or molecule.

concepts.name: Polarizability
concepts.statement: Polarizability is a measure of how easily a charge can distort the electron cloud of an atom or molecule. Larger atoms and molecules, whose valence electrons are held less tightly, are more polarizable.

concepts.name: Viscosity
concepts.statement: The viscosity of a liquid is its resistance to flow. It is greater for liquids of structurally complex molecules with strong intermolecular forces, and it decreases as the temperature rises and the molecules move more rapidly.

concepts.name: Cohesive and adhesive forces
concepts.statement: Cohesive forces are the attractions between identical molecules of a liquid; adhesive forces are the attractions between the liquid and different molecules, such as those of a surface. Their relative strength decides whether a liquid wets a surface and which way its meniscus curves.

concepts.name: Surface tension
concepts.statement: Molecules at the surface of a liquid are attracted by only about half as many neighbors as molecules within it, so the liquid contracts to the smallest surface. Surface tension is the energy required to increase the surface area of a liquid; it makes a small drop spherical and lets a water strider stand on water.

concepts.name: Capillary action
concepts.statement: When the adhesive forces between a liquid and a narrow tube or porous material are strong, combined with the cohesive forces within the liquid, the liquid flows upward against gravity until its weight balances the attraction. The narrower the tube, the higher the liquid climbs.

concepts.name: Capillary rise
concepts.statement: The height to which a liquid rises in a capillary tube is directly proportional to its surface tension and to the cosine of the contact angle, and inversely proportional to the radius of the tube and the density of the liquid. For water in glass the contact angle is 0°.

forms.condition: a liquid in a capillary tube of radius r

concepts.name: Cohesive force
concepts.statement: A cohesive force is a force of attraction between identical molecules, such as the molecules of a liquid.

concepts.name: Adhesive force
concepts.statement: An adhesive force is a force of attraction between molecules of different chemical identities, such as a liquid and the surface it touches.

concepts.name: Vapor pressure and dynamic equilibrium
concepts.statement: In a closed container, a liquid vaporizes until the rate of condensation equals the rate of vaporization; the amounts of liquid and vapor then stop changing, though molecules continue to be exchanged. The pressure of the vapor in this dynamic equilibrium is the liquid’s vapor pressure, and it does not depend on the surface area or the size of the vessel.

concepts.name: Vapor pressure and intermolecular forces
concepts.statement: Strong intermolecular attractions impede vaporization and favor the recapture of gas molecules, so a liquid with stronger forces has a lower vapor pressure.

concepts.name: Vapor pressure rises with temperature
concepts.statement: At a higher temperature a greater fraction of the molecules have enough kinetic energy to escape the liquid, and those that escape move faster, so the vapor pressure increases.

concepts.name: Boiling point and normal boiling point
concepts.statement: A liquid boils when its vapor pressure equals the pressure of the gas above it, so its boiling point depends on the surrounding pressure; the normal boiling point is the boiling point at 1 atm (101.3 kPa). A vapor pressure curve can be read as the boiling point at each pressure.

concepts.name: Clausius-Clapeyron equation
concepts.statement: The vapor pressure of a liquid depends exponentially on temperature, $P = Ae^{-\Delta H_{\text{vap}}/RT}$, so a plot of ln P against 1/T is a straight line whose slope is −ΔH<sub>vap</sub>/R. Temperature must be in kelvin.

forms.condition: the vapor pressure of a liquid, with T in kelvin
the logarithmic, linear form

concepts.name: Using the two-point Clausius-Clapeyron equation
concepts.statement: Given the vapor pressure at two temperatures, we can solve the two-point form for the enthalpy of vaporization; given one pair and the enthalpy of vaporization, we can find the vapor pressure at another temperature or the boiling point at another pressure.

forms.condition: two vapor pressure-temperature pairs of one liquid

concepts.name: Enthalpies of phase change
concepts.statement: Melting, vaporization and sublimation are endothermic, and freezing, condensation and deposition release the same heat with the opposite sign. Melting only partly overcomes the intermolecular attractions while vaporization overcomes them completely, so ΔH<sub>fus</sub> is less than ΔH<sub>vap</sub>, and by Hess’s law ΔH<sub>sub</sub> is about their sum.

forms.condition: sublimation modeled as melting followed by vaporization (Hess's law)

concepts.name: Heating and cooling curves
concepts.statement: As a substance is heated at a steady rate, its temperature rises within each phase, as q = mcΔT describes, and stays constant at each phase transition while the heat goes into overcoming intermolecular attractions. The plateaus of a heating curve are its phase transitions.

concepts.name: Calculating heat from a heating curve
concepts.statement: The heat for a change through several phases is the sum of the steps: q = mcΔT for each warming or cooling within a phase, with the specific heat of that phase, and q = nΔH for each transition.

concepts.name: Vaporization
concepts.statement: Vaporization is the change from the liquid state to the gaseous state.

concepts.name: Condensation
concepts.statement: Condensation is the change from the gaseous state to the liquid state.

concepts.name: Melting
concepts.statement: Melting is the change from the solid state to the liquid state.

concepts.name: Freezing
concepts.statement: Freezing is the change from the liquid state to the solid state.

concepts.name: Sublimation
concepts.statement: Sublimation is the change from the solid state directly to the gaseous state.

concepts.name: Deposition
concepts.statement: Deposition is the change from the gaseous state directly to the solid state.

concepts.name: Dynamic equilibrium
concepts.statement: A dynamic equilibrium is the state of a system in which reciprocal processes occur at equal rates, so that nothing changes overall although both processes continue.

concepts.name: Vapor pressure
concepts.statement: The vapor pressure, or equilibrium vapor pressure, of a liquid or solid is the pressure exerted by its vapor in equilibrium with it at a given temperature.

concepts.name: Normal boiling point
concepts.statement: The normal boiling point of a liquid is the temperature at which its vapor pressure equals 1 atm (760 torr).

concepts.name: Melting point and freezing point
concepts.statement: The melting point of a substance is the temperature at which its solid and liquid phases are in equilibrium. The same temperature is called the freezing point when it is reached by cooling the liquid.

concepts.name: Phase diagrams
concepts.statement: A phase diagram combines the pressure-temperature curves of the liquid-gas, solid-liquid and solid-gas equilibria of a substance. Each region is the phase that is stable under those conditions, and each curve gives a transition temperature as a function of pressure.

concepts.name: Reading a phase diagram
concepts.statement: To find the state of a substance, we locate the temperature and pressure on its phase diagram and read the region; to find the phase changes on heating at constant pressure, or on compression at constant temperature, we follow a horizontal or vertical line and note the curves it crosses.

concepts.name: Triple point
concepts.statement: The triple point is the temperature and pressure at which the solid, liquid and gas phases are in equilibrium. Below the triple-point pressure a substance cannot exist as a liquid, so it sublimes; freeze-drying and dry ice depend on this.

concepts.name: Slope of the solid-liquid curve
concepts.statement: For most substances the solid-liquid curve has a positive slope, so the melting point rises with pressure; for water it has a slight negative slope, so pressure lowers the melting point of ice.

concepts.name: Critical point and supercritical fluid
concepts.statement: The liquid-gas curve ends at the critical point. Above the critical temperature, no amount of pressure can liquefy a gas, and the substance is a supercritical fluid, with properties between those of a liquid and a gas.

concepts.name: Critical point
concepts.statement: The critical point of a substance is the temperature and pressure above which its gas cannot be condensed into a liquid, the point at which its liquid-gas curve ends.

concepts.name: Supercritical fluid
concepts.statement: A supercritical fluid is a substance at a temperature and pressure higher than its critical point, with properties between those of a gas and a liquid.

concepts.name: Crystalline and amorphous solids
concepts.statement: In a crystalline solid, the particles are arranged in a definite repeating pattern. Every particle is held by the same forces, so the solid melts at a precise temperature. In an amorphous solid, the particles are arranged randomly and the attractions vary, so the solid softens over a range of temperatures.

concepts.name: Types of crystalline solids
concepts.statement: Crystalline solids are classified by the forces between their particles, and these forces explain their properties: ionic solids are hard, brittle and conduct only when molten; metallic solids are malleable conductors; covalent network solids are very hard with very high melting points; molecular solids are soft with low melting points.

concepts.name: Classifying a crystalline solid
concepts.statement: From a formula we identify the particles (ions, metal atoms, network-forming atoms or molecules) and so the type of solid; from observed properties such as hardness, conductivity and melting point we reason back to the type.

concepts.name: Crystal defects
concepts.statement: The repeating pattern of a crystal may contain defects: vacancies where a particle is missing, particles in interstitial sites, and impurities substituted into the lattice. Defects change physical properties, and doping silicon for semiconductors introduces them deliberately.

concepts.name: Crystalline solid
concepts.statement: A crystalline solid is a solid in which the particles are arranged in a definite repeating pattern.

concepts.name: Amorphous solid
concepts.statement: An amorphous solid, or noncrystalline solid, is a solid in which the particles lack an ordered internal structure.

concepts.name: Ionic solid
concepts.statement: An ionic solid is a crystalline solid composed of positive and negative ions held together by strong electrostatic attractions.

concepts.name: Metallic solid
concepts.statement: A metallic solid is a crystalline solid composed of metal atoms.

concepts.name: Covalent network solid
concepts.statement: A covalent network solid is a crystalline solid whose particles are held together by covalent bonds.

concepts.name: Molecular solid
concepts.statement: A molecular solid is a crystalline solid composed of neutral molecules held together by intermolecular forces of attraction.

concepts.name: Vacancy
concepts.statement: A vacancy is a defect in a crystal where a position that should contain an atom or ion is empty.

concepts.name: Interstitial sites
concepts.statement: Interstitial sites are the spaces between the regular particle positions in an array of atoms or ions.

concepts.name: Unit cell
concepts.statement: The structure of a crystal is described by its unit cell, its simplest repeating unit, whose lattice points mark the locations of atoms or ions and which repeats in three dimensions. A unit cell is defined by three edge lengths and three angles, giving seven lattice systems and fourteen unit cells.

concepts.name: Cubic unit cells
concepts.statement: Counting one-eighth of each corner atom, one-half of each face atom and all of a body-center atom, a simple cubic cell contains one atom, a body-centered cubic cell two and a face-centered cubic cell four. Their coordination numbers are 6, 8 and 12, and they fill about 52%, 68% and 74% of the space.

concepts.name: Hexagonal and cubic closest packing
concepts.statement: Identical spheres pack most closely in hexagonal layers, each layer sitting in the hollows of the one below. Stacking ABAB… gives hexagonal closest packing and ABCABC… gives cubic closest packing, which is the face-centered cubic structure; both have a coordination number of 12, and about two-thirds of metals crystallize this way.

concepts.name: Finding radius and density from a unit cell
concepts.statement: Where the atoms touch (along an edge in a simple cubic cell, along a face diagonal in a face-centered cubic cell, along a body diagonal in a body-centered one) the edge length gives the radius; the atoms per cell times the mass of an atom, divided by the cell’s volume, gives the density. The same geometry gives ionic radii from the edge length of an ionic crystal.

concepts.name: Holes in closest-packed arrays
concepts.statement: In simple ionic structures the larger anions usually form a closest-packed array and the smaller cations occupy the holes between them: tetrahedral holes, two per anion, for small cations; octahedral holes, one per anion, for larger ones; and cubic holes in a simple cubic array for the largest.

concepts.name: Finding a formula from hole occupancy
concepts.statement: Knowing the number of holes of each kind per anion, the fraction of them the cations occupy gives the ratio of cations to anions, and so the formula of the compound.

concepts.name: Unit cells of ionic compounds
concepts.statement: Ionic compounds with ions of similar size in a 1:1 ratio, such as CsCl, form a simple cubic structure; those whose ions differ more in size, such as NaCl and ZnS, form a face-centered cubic cell with the cations in octahedral or tetrahedral holes; CaF₂ is face-centered cubic with fluoride ions in all the tetrahedral holes. The contents of the cell give the formula.

concepts.name: Bragg equation
concepts.statement: X-rays scattered by atoms in adjacent crystal planes interfere constructively only when the extra distance traveled is a whole number of wavelengths, which happens at the angle given by the Bragg equation; measuring the diffraction angles gives the spacing of the planes.

forms.condition: constructive interference of X-rays scattered by planes a distance d apart

concepts.name: Space lattice
concepts.statement: The space lattice of a crystal is the set of all points within it that have identical environments.

concepts.name: Coordination number
concepts.statement: The coordination number of an atom in a crystal is the number of atoms closest to it; in a complex, it is the number of atoms bonded to the central metal atom.

concepts.name: Simple cubic unit cell
concepts.statement: A simple cubic unit cell, or primitive cubic unit cell, is a cube with lattice points only at its corners, the unit cell of the simple cubic structure.

concepts.name: Simple cubic structure
concepts.statement: The simple cubic structure is a crystalline structure whose cubic unit cell has lattice points only at the corners.

concepts.name: Body-centered cubic unit cell
concepts.statement: A body-centered cubic unit cell is the simplest repeating unit of a body-centered cubic crystal, a cube with lattice points at each corner and at its center.

concepts.name: Body-centered cubic solid
concepts.statement: A body-centered cubic solid is a crystalline structure whose cubic unit cell has lattice points at the corners and in the center of the cell.

concepts.name: Face-centered cubic unit cell
concepts.statement: A face-centered cubic unit cell is the simplest repeating unit of a face-centered cubic crystal, a cube with lattice points at each corner and at the center of each face.

concepts.name: Face-centered cubic solid
concepts.statement: A face-centered cubic solid is a crystalline structure whose cubic unit cell has lattice points on the corners and in the center of each face.

concepts.name: Isomorphous
concepts.statement: Substances are isomorphous when they possess the same crystalline structure.

concepts.name: Hexagonal closest packing
concepts.statement: Hexagonal closest packing is a crystalline structure in which closely packed layers of atoms or ions are stacked in two alternating layers, ABAB….

concepts.name: Cubic closest packing
concepts.statement: Cubic closest packing is a crystalline structure in which closely packed layers of atoms or ions are stacked in three alternating layers, ABCABC…; its unit cell is face-centered cubic.

concepts.name: Hole
concepts.statement: A hole, or interstice, is a space between the atoms or ions of a crystal.

concepts.name: Tetrahedral hole
concepts.statement: A tetrahedral hole is the space formed by four atoms or ions of a crystal at the corners of a tetrahedron.

concepts.name: Octahedral hole
concepts.statement: An octahedral hole is the open space in a crystal at the center of six particles located at the corners of an octahedron.

concepts.name: Diffraction
concepts.statement: Diffraction is the redirection of electromagnetic radiation when it encounters a physical barrier of dimensions similar to its wavelength.

concepts.name: X-ray crystallography
concepts.statement: X-ray crystallography is the experimental technique that finds the distances between the atoms of a crystal by measuring the angles at which X-rays are diffracted as they pass through it.

concepts.name: Chemical equations
concepts.statement: A chemical equation represents a reaction symbolically: the formulas of the reactants on the left, the formulas of the products on the right, plus signs between formulas and an arrow between the two sides. Parenthetical abbreviations give the physical state of each substance (s, l, g, aq), and a word or symbol over the arrow, such as Δ for heating, names a special condition.

concepts.name: Coefficients give relative numbers
concepts.statement: The coefficients of a balanced equation state the relative numbers of reactant and product species, so they may be read as ratios in any amount unit: one molecule of methane and two of oxygen, one dozen and two dozen, or one mole and two moles. Note that the convention is to use the smallest whole-number coefficients, and that this reading is what makes an equation a statement about amounts rather than only about identities.

concepts.name: A balanced equation conserves atoms
concepts.statement: An equation is balanced when equal numbers of atoms of each element are represented on the reactant and product sides, which is what the law of conservation of matter requires. The number of atoms of an element is the coefficient of each formula containing it multiplied by the element's subscript in that formula, added over every formula on that side.

concepts.name: Balancing an equation by inspection
concepts.statement: Balancing by inspection changes coefficients, never subscripts, one element at a time until every element balances; changing a subscript would change the identity of a substance, as turning H2O into H2O2 turns water into hydrogen peroxide. A fractional coefficient may be used along the way and then cleared by multiplying through by a whole number.

concepts.name: Ionic equations
concepts.statement: A reaction between ionic compounds in water may be written with different levels of detail. A molecular equation writes every substance as a neutral formula; a complete ionic equation writes the dissolved ionic compounds as their dissociated ions; and a net ionic equation leaves out the spectator ions, which appear unchanged on both sides, so that it shows only the species that actually change.

concepts.name: Writing a net ionic equation
concepts.statement: Start from a balanced molecular equation. Dissociate every dissolved ionic compound into its ions, find the spectator ions present in identical form on both sides, remove them, and reduce the coefficients to the smallest whole numbers. The result says, for example, that solid silver chloride forms from dissolved silver and chloride ions whatever their source.

concepts.name: Reactant
concepts.statement: A reactant is a substance undergoing a chemical or physical change, shown on the left side of the arrow in a chemical equation.

concepts.name: Product
concepts.statement: A product is a substance formed by a chemical or physical change, shown on the right side of the arrow in a chemical equation.

concepts.name: Coefficient
concepts.statement: A coefficient is a number placed in front of a symbol or formula in a chemical equation to indicate its relative amount.

concepts.name: Molecular equation
concepts.statement: A molecular equation is a chemical equation in which all reactants and products are represented as neutral substances.

concepts.name: Complete ionic equation
concepts.statement: A complete ionic equation is a chemical equation in which all dissolved ionic reactants and products, including spectator ions, are explicitly represented by formulas for their dissociated ions.

concepts.name: Net ionic equation
concepts.statement: A net ionic equation is a chemical equation in which only those dissolved ionic reactants and products that undergo a chemical or physical change are represented, so spectator ions are excluded.

concepts.name: Spectator ion
concepts.statement: A spectator ion is an ion that does not undergo a chemical or physical change during a reaction, but its presence is required to maintain charge neutrality.

concepts.name: Precipitation reactions and solubility
concepts.statement: A precipitation reaction is one in which dissolved substances react to form one or more solid products, often by an exchange of ions between ionic compounds. A substance precipitates when its concentration exceeds its solubility, the maximum concentration that can be achieved under specified conditions, so the insoluble compounds are the ones that come out of solution.

concepts.name: Predicting a precipitate from solubility guidelines
concepts.statement: To predict whether mixing two solutions gives a precipitate, identify every ion present, consider each new cation and anion pairing, and look each up in the solubility guidelines. If one pairing is insoluble, a precipitation reaction is expected and its net ionic equation can be written.

concepts.name: Acids and bases
concepts.statement: An acid-base reaction is one in which a hydrogen ion is transferred from one species to another. In water, an acid is a substance that yields hydronium ions, as hydrogen chloride does by transferring H+ to water molecules, and a base is one that yields hydroxide ions, either by dissociating, as ionic hydroxides do, or by reacting with water, as ammonia does.

concepts.name: Strong and weak acids and bases
concepts.statement: A strong acid reacts completely with water, so virtually every dissolved molecule yields a hydronium ion, and a strong base, such as an ionic hydroxide, dissociates completely. A weak acid or weak base reacts only partially and leaves most of its molecules in their original form, which is why its equation carries a double arrow. Under typical conditions only about 1% of acetic acid or of ammonia ionizes.

concepts.name: Neutralization reactions
concepts.statement: A neutralization reaction is an acid-base reaction whose reactants are an acid and a base (but not water), and whose products are often a salt and water. The net ionic equation for the neutralization of any strong acid by an ionic hydroxide is the same, hydronium ion and hydroxide ion giving water.

concepts.name: Assigning oxidation numbers
concepts.statement: The oxidation number of an element in a compound is the charge its atoms would have if the compound were ionic. Four guidelines assign it: zero in an elemental substance, the ion's charge for a monatomic ion, the usual values for hydrogen, oxygen and the halogens, and a sum equal to the charge of the molecule or ion, which fixes the one unknown. An oxidation number puts the sign first (+2), and a charge puts the number first (2+).

concepts.name: Oxidation-reduction reactions
concepts.statement: An oxidation-reduction (redox) reaction is one in which one or more elements undergo a change in oxidation number. Oxidation is an increase in oxidation number, or a loss of electrons, and reduction a decrease, or a gain; the reducing agent is the species oxidized and the oxidizing agent the species reduced. Defined this way, the class includes reactions such as hydrogen with chlorine in which no electrons are transferred outright.

concepts.name: Classifying a reaction
concepts.statement: From an equation or a description, say whether a reaction is a precipitation, an acid-base or a redox reaction, or more than one. Where a redox subclass fits, name it. In combustion, a fuel and an oxidant react vigorously to give heat and often light. In single displacement, the oxidation of a metal replaces an ion in solution. In disproportionation, one element is both oxidized and reduced.

concepts.name: Balancing redox equations by half-reactions
concepts.statement: A redox equation in aqueous solution can be hard to balance by inspection because water, hydronium ions and hydroxide ions take part. The half-reaction method writes the oxidation and the reduction separately, balances each for atoms (oxygen with water, hydrogen with H+) and then for charge with electrons, scales them to equal numbers of electrons and adds them, with extra steps that convert H+ to water in basic solution. Both atoms and charge must balance at the end.

concepts.name: Solubility
concepts.statement: The solubility of a substance is the extent to which it dissolves in water or any other solvent. A substance of relatively high solubility is soluble, and one that dissolves only to a slight extent is insoluble.

concepts.name: Salt
concepts.statement: A salt is an ionic compound that can be formed by the reaction of an acid with a base, containing a cation and an anion other than hydroxide or oxide.

concepts.name: Combustion reaction
concepts.statement: A combustion reaction is a vigorous redox reaction producing significant amounts of energy in the form of heat and, sometimes, light.

concepts.name: Single-displacement reaction
concepts.statement: A single-displacement (replacement) reaction is a redox reaction in which an elemental substance is oxidized by an ionic species.

concepts.name: Half-reaction
concepts.statement: A half-reaction is an equation that shows either the oxidation or the reduction of a redox reaction alone, with the electrons each reactant loses or gains.

concepts.name: Soluble
concepts.statement: A soluble substance is one of relatively high solubility, dissolving to a relatively large extent.

concepts.name: Insoluble
concepts.statement: An insoluble substance is one of relatively low solubility, dissolving only to a slight extent.

concepts.name: Precipitate
concepts.statement: A precipitate is an insoluble product that forms from the reaction of soluble reactants.

concepts.name: Acid
concepts.statement: An acid is a substance that produces H₃O⁺ when dissolved in water.

concepts.name: Base
concepts.statement: A base is a substance that produces OH⁻ when dissolved in water.

concepts.name: Acid-base reaction
concepts.statement: An acid-base reaction is a reaction involving the transfer of a hydrogen ion between reactant species.

concepts.name: Strong acid
concepts.statement: A strong acid is an acid that reacts completely when dissolved in water to yield hydronium ions.

concepts.name: Weak acid
concepts.statement: A weak acid is an acid that reacts only to a slight extent when dissolved in water to yield hydronium ions.

concepts.name: Strong base
concepts.statement: A strong base is a base that reacts completely when dissolved in water to yield hydroxide ions.

concepts.name: Weak base
concepts.statement: A weak base is a base that reacts only to a slight extent when dissolved in water to yield hydroxide ions.

concepts.name: Oxidation number
concepts.statement: The oxidation number, or oxidation state, of an element in a compound is the charge each of its atoms would have if the compound were ionic.

concepts.name: Oxidation
concepts.statement: Oxidation is the process in which an element’s oxidation number is increased by loss of electrons.

concepts.name: Reduction
concepts.statement: Reduction is the process in which an element’s oxidation number is decreased by gain of electrons.

concepts.name: Oxidizing agent
concepts.statement: An oxidizing agent, or oxidant, is a substance that brings about the oxidation of another substance and in the process becomes reduced.

concepts.name: Reducing agent
concepts.statement: A reducing agent, or reductant, is a substance that brings about the reduction of another substance and in the process becomes oxidized.

concepts.name: Reaction stoichiometry
concepts.statement: The stoichiometry of a reaction is the set of quantitative relationships between the amounts of the substances it consumes and produces, and the balanced equation states it. As a recipe for eight pancakes scales to twenty-four, the coefficients scale to any amount of any reactant or product.

concepts.name: Stoichiometric factors
concepts.statement: A stoichiometric factor is a ratio of two coefficients from a balanced equation, such as 2 mol NH3 per 3 mol H2 in the synthesis of ammonia, and you can write it in any amount unit. It is the one step every reaction stoichiometry calculation shares, whatever quantities it starts from and asks for.

concepts.name: Mole stoichiometry
concepts.statement: Multiplying a given molar amount of one substance by the stoichiometric factor gives the molar amount of another, and Avogadro's number turns that molar amount into a number of molecules. This is the shortest stoichiometry calculation and the pattern the longer ones extend.

concepts.name: Mass stoichiometry
concepts.statement: Since masses, not numbers of molecules, are what can be measured, a practical stoichiometry calculation converts a given mass (or a volume of a solution of known molarity) to moles, applies the stoichiometric factor, and converts the result back to a mass or a volume. The route is the same whether the two substances are a reactant and a product or two reactants.

concepts.name: Limiting and excess reactants
concepts.statement: When reactants are not present in stoichiometric amounts, one runs out first and limits the amount of product. The others are in excess, and some of each remains. Eleven slices of cheese and twenty-eight slices of bread make eleven sandwiches with six slices of bread to spare, and three moles of hydrogen with two of chlorine make four moles of hydrogen chloride with one mole of hydrogen to spare.

concepts.name: Identifying the limiting reactant
concepts.statement: There are two ways. Compare the molar ratio of the reactants provided with the stoichiometric ratio of the equation, or compute the amount of product each reactant alone would give; the reactant that gives the lesser amount is the limiting one.

concepts.name: Theoretical and actual yield
concepts.statement: The theoretical yield is the amount of product the stoichiometry of the balanced equation predicts from the limiting reactant; the actual yield is the amount obtained, and it is often less because of side reactions, incomplete reactions and losses in collecting the product.

concepts.name: Percent yield
concepts.statement: Percent yield is the actual yield divided by the theoretical yield, times 100%, and it measures how efficiently a reaction delivered the product the stoichiometry allows. Both yields may be masses, molar amounts or any other measure, so long as they are in the same units, which then cancel.

concepts.name: Atom economy
concepts.statement: The atom economy of a process is the mass of the desired product as a percentage of the mass of all the reactants used, a measure of how much of what goes in ends up in the product. It looks like percent yield but compares the theoretical efficiencies of different processes, whereas percent yield compares what one process actually gives with what it could give.

forms.condition: the theoretical efficiency of a synthesis, the mass of the desired product as a percentage of the mass of all the reactants used

concepts.name: Theoretical yield
concepts.statement: The theoretical yield is the amount of product that may be produced from a given amount of reactant according to the reaction stoichiometry.

concepts.name: Actual yield
concepts.statement: The actual yield is the amount of product formed in a reaction.

concepts.name: Excess reactant
concepts.statement: An excess reactant is a reactant present in an amount greater than required by the reaction stoichiometry.

concepts.name: Quantitative chemical analysis
