concepts.statement: Quantitative analysis is the determination of the amount or concentration of a substance in a sample, and reaction stoichiometry is one of its foundations: the amount of a reactant that combines with the analyte, or of a product it gives, measures how much analyte there was.

concepts.name: Titration analysis
concepts.statement: In a titration, a titrant of known concentration is added from a buret to a sample of the analyte until the reaction between them is complete. The volume of titrant needed to reach this equivalence point, detected as an end point by a change such as an indicator's color, measures the amount of analyte through the reaction's stoichiometry.

concepts.name: Calculating a concentration from titration data
concepts.statement: The volume and molarity of the titrant give its molar amount, the stoichiometric factor gives the molar amount of analyte, and dividing by the sample volume gives the analyte's molarity. Since molarity is also millimoles per milliliter, the calculation can be done in milliliters throughout.

concepts.name: Gravimetric analysis
concepts.statement: In a gravimetric analysis the analyte is separated from the sample by a change of state, often by precipitation and filtration, and weighed; the mass of the isolated substance, carried through the stoichiometry, gives the mass of the analyte and its percent of the sample.

concepts.name: Combustion analysis
concepts.statement: A weighed sample of a compound of carbon and hydrogen is burned completely in oxygen, and the carbon dioxide and water it gives are collected in separate preweighed absorbers. The mass of each product gives the moles of carbon and of hydrogen in the sample, and their smallest whole-number ratio gives the empirical formula.

concepts.name: Analyte
concepts.statement: An analyte is the chemical species of interest in an analysis.

concepts.name: Titrant
concepts.statement: A titrant is a solution containing a known concentration of a substance that will react with the analyte in a titration analysis.

concepts.name: Buret
concepts.statement: A buret is a device used for the precise delivery of variable liquid volumes, as in a titration analysis.

concepts.name: Equivalence point
concepts.statement: The equivalence point is the volume of titrant solution required to react completely with the analyte in a titration analysis, a stoichiometric amount of titrant for the sample’s analyte.

concepts.name: End point
concepts.statement: The end point is the measured volume of titrant solution that yields the change in the sample’s appearance or other property expected for stoichiometric equivalence.

concepts.name: Indicator
concepts.statement: An indicator is a substance added to the sample in a titration analysis to permit visual detection of the end point.

concepts.name: Energy
concepts.statement: Energy is the capacity to supply heat or do work. Work is one of the two things energy does: moving matter against an opposing force, as a pump does when it pushes air into a tire.

concepts.name: Potential energy and kinetic energy
concepts.statement: Energy can be sorted into two kinds: potential energy, which an object has because of its position, composition, or condition, and kinetic energy, which it has because of its motion. The chemical energy stored in gasoline is potential energy, and thermal energy is kinetic energy.

concepts.name: Law of conservation of energy
concepts.statement: During a chemical or physical change, energy can be neither created nor destroyed, although it can be changed in form. The heat a reaction gives off must therefore turn up somewhere else.

concepts.name: Thermal energy and temperature
concepts.statement: Thermal energy is the kinetic energy of the random motion of atoms and molecules, and temperature is a measure of how hot or cold a sample is, which rises as the average kinetic energy of its particles rises. The two are not the same thing: a bonfire and a match may share a temperature and hold very different amounts of thermal energy.

concepts.name: Heat
concepts.statement: Heat is the transfer of thermal energy between two bodies at different temperatures. It flows spontaneously from the hotter body to the cooler one, lowering the average kinetic energy of the first and raising that of the second, until the two reach thermal equilibrium at one temperature.

concepts.name: Exothermic and endothermic processes
concepts.statement: A chemical reaction or physical change that releases heat is exothermic, and one that absorbs heat is endothermic. An exothermic process warms its surroundings, and an endothermic process cools them.

concepts.name: Converting energy units
concepts.statement: The SI unit of energy is the joule, but chemists still frequently use the calorie, and food labels give energy in Calories, each of which is a kilocalorie. One calorie is exactly 4.184 joules. Move between these units with ease to read a food label or to compare results given in either.

concepts.name: Heat capacity and specific heat
concepts.statement: The heat capacity of a body is the heat it absorbs or releases for a temperature change of 1 °C, and it grows with the amount of material, so it is extensive. The specific heat is the heat needed to raise 1 gram of a substance by 1 °C, and it depends only on the kind of substance, so it is intensive.

concepts.name: Heat and specific heat
concepts.statement: The heat entering or leaving a substance is the product of its specific heat, its mass, and its temperature change, taken as the final temperature minus the initial one. The sign of q follows from that difference, positive when the substance warms and negative when it cools, and any one of the four quantities can be found when the other three are known.

forms.condition: no chemical reaction or phase change occurs, and the specific heat is treated as constant over the temperature range

concepts.name: Thermochemistry
concepts.statement: Thermochemistry is the study of measuring the amount of heat absorbed or released during a chemical reaction or a physical change.

concepts.name: Work
concepts.statement: Work is the transfer of energy that moves matter against an opposing force, or that changes external, macroscopic variables such as pressure and volume.

concepts.name: Potential energy
concepts.statement: Potential energy is the energy a particle or a system of particles has because of its relative position, composition, or condition.

concepts.name: Kinetic energy
concepts.statement: Kinetic energy is the energy an object has because of its motion, equal to one-half the product of its mass and the square of its velocity.

forms.condition: a particle of mass m moving at speed u

concepts.name: Thermal energy
concepts.statement: Thermal energy is the kinetic energy associated with the random motion of atoms and molecules.

concepts.name: Exothermic process
concepts.statement: An exothermic process is a chemical reaction or physical change that releases heat.

concepts.name: Endothermic process
concepts.statement: An endothermic process is a chemical reaction or physical change that absorbs heat.

concepts.name: Joule
concepts.statement: The joule is the SI unit of energy, the energy used when a force of 1 newton moves an object 1 meter.

concepts.name: Calorie
concepts.statement: The calorie is a unit of heat or other energy, the amount of energy required to raise 1 gram of water by 1 degree Celsius. One calorie is exactly 4.184 joules.

concepts.name: Heat capacity
concepts.statement: The heat capacity of a body of matter is the quantity of heat required to raise its temperature by 1 degree Celsius. It is an extensive property, growing with the amount of matter in the body.

forms.condition: a body of matter that absorbs or releases heat q with no chemical reaction or phase change

concepts.name: Specific heat capacity
concepts.statement: The specific heat capacity of a substance is the quantity of heat required to raise the temperature of 1 gram of it by 1 degree Celsius. It is an intensive property, set by the kind of substance alone.

forms.condition: a sample of one substance with no chemical reaction or phase change

concepts.name: System and surroundings
concepts.statement: The system is the portion of matter undergoing the chemical or physical change being studied, and the surroundings are everything else that gives heat to the system or takes it away. The sign of a heat is taken from the system's point of view.

concepts.name: Calorimeter heat balance
concepts.statement: When a hot metal is placed in cool water in an ideal calorimeter, all the heat lost by one is gained by the other, so the two heats add up to zero and one is the negative of the other. The negative sign records the opposite direction of flow and does not by itself give either value its sign.

forms.condition: an ideal calorimeter, in which all the heat transfer occurs between the two substances

concepts.name: Heat of reaction by calorimetry
concepts.statement: Because energy is neither created nor destroyed, the heat produced or consumed by a reaction in a calorimeter equals the heat absorbed or lost by the solution around it, with the opposite sign. This is the concept that lies at the heart of all calorimetry problems: the temperature change of the solution is measured, and the heat of the reaction is read from it.

forms.condition: the calorimeter absorbs no heat and exchanges none with the outside environment

concepts.name: Coffee cup calorimetry
concepts.statement: A coffee cup calorimeter measures a temperature change, and turning it into a heat takes reasonable assumptions, stated openly. No heat passes to the outside or into the cup, and a dilute solution has the specific heat and density of water. Carry those assumptions through to a heat with the right sign.

concepts.name: Bomb calorimetry
concepts.statement: A bomb calorimeter works at constant volume and is used for reactions, such as combustions, that give off much heat and gaseous products. The heat of the reaction is shared between the water and the steel bomb, so the calculation adds the heat taken in by the water to the heat capacity of the bomb times the temperature rise.

forms.condition: a bomb calorimeter, with the heat absorbed by the products and the excess oxygen neglected

concepts.name: Counting the Calories in a food
concepts.statement: Food labels give energy in Calories. The Atwater system computes them from the grams of protein, carbohydrate, and fat in a serving and their average Calories per gram, values that came from bomb calorimetry. With this sum you can check a label and compare foods.

concepts.name: System
concepts.statement: The system is the portion of matter undergoing the chemical or physical change being studied.

concepts.name: Surroundings
concepts.statement: The surroundings are all the matter other than the system being studied.

concepts.name: Calorimetry
concepts.statement: Calorimetry is the process of measuring the amount of heat involved in a chemical or physical process.

concepts.name: Calorimeter
concepts.statement: A calorimeter is a device used to measure the amount of heat absorbed or released in a chemical or physical process.

concepts.name: Bomb calorimeter
concepts.statement: A bomb calorimeter is a device designed to measure the energy change of a process at constant volume. It is commonly used for reactions, such as combustions, that release large amounts of heat and gaseous products.

concepts.name: Nutritional Calorie
concepts.statement: The nutritional Calorie is the unit used for the energy provided by digestion of foods, defined as 1000 calories, or 1 kilocalorie.

concepts.name: First law of thermodynamics
concepts.statement: The internal energy of a system changes only through heat flowing into or out of it and work done on or by it. The signs take the system's side: q is positive for heat flowing in and w is positive for work done on the system. A system that loses heat and does work therefore loses internal energy on both counts, as the gases in an engine cylinder do.

concepts.name: State functions
concepts.statement: The value of a state function depends only on the state a system is in, and not on how that state was reached. Internal energy and enthalpy are state functions, while heat and work are not, just as the altitude of a summit does not depend on the route climbed but the distance walked does. Hess's law rests on this property.

concepts.name: Enthalpy change at constant pressure
concepts.statement: Enthalpy is the sum of a system's internal energy and the product of its pressure and volume. For a process at constant pressure whose only work is expansion work, the enthalpy change equals the heat flow, which is why chemists, who usually work at the constant pressure of the atmosphere, use enthalpy to describe the heat of a reaction. The heat measured in a bomb calorimeter, at constant volume, is not ΔH.

forms.condition: a process at constant pressure whose only work is caused by expansion or contraction

concepts.name: Writing and scaling thermochemical equations
concepts.statement: A thermochemical equation gives ΔH after a balanced equation, for the amounts in moles that the equation shows. Since ΔH is extensive, it scales with the coefficients. It changes sign when you reverse the equation, and it depends on the physical states written. Apply all three rules, and account for the limiting reactant when you turn a measured heat into ΔH.

concepts.name: Using a standard enthalpy of combustion
concepts.statement: The standard enthalpy of combustion is the enthalpy change when 1 mole of a substance burns completely under standard state conditions. With it, and with the conversions of earlier chapters, you can find the heat given by any amount of a fuel, as the value for isooctane gives the heat of 1.00 L of gasoline.

concepts.name: Standard enthalpy of formation
concepts.statement: A standard state is an agreed set of reference conditions, 1 bar and 1 M, with 298.15 K assumed, and ΔH° marks an enthalpy change under them. The standard enthalpy of formation is ΔH° for forming exactly 1 mole of a substance from its elements in their most stable states, so an element in its most stable form has a value of zero and the formation equation often carries fractional coefficients.

concepts.name: Hess’s law
concepts.statement: If a process is the sum of several stepwise processes, the enthalpy change of the total process equals the sum of the enthalpy changes of the steps. You can then find the enthalpy change of a reaction that is hard or dangerous to carry out by adding reactions of known enthalpy change, reversed and scaled as needed.

concepts.name: Finding a reaction enthalpy from formation enthalpies
concepts.statement: Apply Hess's law by decomposing the reactants into their elements and re-forming the products. The standard enthalpy change of any reaction is then the sum of n times the enthalpies of formation of the products minus the same sum for the reactants. With the table of Appendix G you can compute ΔH° for reactions that no one has measured directly.

forms.condition: standard state conditions, with n the stoichiometric coefficients of the balanced equation

concepts.name: Chemical thermodynamics
concepts.statement: Chemical thermodynamics is the area of science that deals with the relationships between heat, work, and all forms of energy associated with chemical and physical processes.

concepts.name: Internal energy
concepts.statement: The internal energy of a system is the total of all possible kinds of energy present in the substances it contains.

concepts.name: Expansion work
concepts.statement: Expansion work, or pressure-volume work, is the work done as a system expands or contracts against an external pressure.

forms.condition: expansion or pressure-volume work

concepts.name: Enthalpy
concepts.statement: The enthalpy of a system is the sum of its internal energy and the product of its pressure and volume.

concepts.name: Enthalpy change
concepts.statement: The enthalpy change of a process is the change in the enthalpy of the system, equal to the heat it releases or absorbs when the process takes place at constant pressure.

forms.condition: a process at constant pressure

concepts.name: Standard state
concepts.statement: A standard state is a set of physical conditions accepted as common reference conditions for reporting thermodynamic properties: 1 bar of pressure and 1 M concentration, with a temperature of 298.15 K assumed. A degree sign on an enthalpy change marks a process under these conditions.

concepts.name: Hydrocarbon
concepts.statement: A hydrocarbon is a compound composed only of hydrogen and carbon, the major component of fossil fuels.

concepts.name: Standard enthalpy of combustion
concepts.statement: The standard enthalpy of combustion of a substance is the enthalpy change when 1 mole of it undergoes complete combustion under standard state conditions.

concepts.name: Calculating formula mass
concepts.statement: You calculate the formula mass of a substance by multiplying each element’s average atomic mass by its subscript and adding the products.

concepts.name: Molecular mass versus formula mass
concepts.statement: For a covalent substance the formula describes one molecule, so its formula mass may be called a molecular mass; an ionic compound has no discrete molecule, so its formula mass may not. The masses of neutral atoms are used for ions as well, since the mass of an electron is negligible beside that of an atom.

concepts.name: Mole
concepts.statement: The mole is an amount unit like a pair or a dozen, and it links an easily measured property, bulk mass, to a fundamental one, the number of atoms or molecules. Chemists count particles they cannot see by weighing them, and the mole is the unit that makes that possible.

concepts.name: Avogadro’s number
concepts.statement: One mole of any substance contains the same number of entities, 6.022 × 10<sup>23</sup>, so the number of atoms or molecules in a sample follows from its amount in moles. The size of the number is what lets a drop of water hold more molecules than can be clearly imagined.

concepts.name: Molar mass
concepts.statement: The molar mass of a substance is the mass in grams of 1 mole of it, and it is numerically equal to the formula mass in amu, because the atomic mass unit and the mole are defined from the same reference, carbon-12. That equality turns a formula mass read from the periodic table into a conversion factor between grams and moles.

concepts.name: Converting between mass and moles
concepts.statement: Dividing a mass by the molar mass gives the amount in moles, and multiplying an amount by the molar mass gives the mass. This is the conversion the rest of the book leans on whenever a quantity weighed on a balance must become a count of particles or the reverse.

concepts.name: Counting atoms and molecules
concepts.statement: A mass is converted to moles with the molar mass and then to a number of entities with Avogadro’s number, and the formula then gives the number of each kind of atom. The two-step chain answers questions no balance can answer directly, such as how many carbon atoms a packet of sweetener holds.

concepts.name: Formula mass
concepts.statement: The formula mass of a substance is the sum of the average masses of all the atoms represented in its chemical formula; for a covalent compound it is also the molecular mass.

concepts.name: Percent composition
concepts.statement: The percent composition of a compound is the percentage by mass of each element in it. Measuring the mass of each element is often the first step in finding an unknown compound’s formula, and the percentages are how that measurement is reported.

forms.condition: X is any one element of the compound

concepts.name: Percent composition from a formula
concepts.statement: When the formula is known, the percent composition follows from the atomic or molar masses alone, by taking one mole of the compound as the sample. This is how a fertilizer buyer compares the nitrogen in ammonia, ammonium nitrate and urea.

concepts.name: Deriving an empirical formula
concepts.statement: A formula states the relative numbers of atoms, not their masses. So convert each element’s mass to moles, divide the amounts by the smallest, and multiply by an integer if needed to reach whole numbers. The procedure turns an analysis on a balance into a chemical formula.

concepts.name: Deriving an empirical formula from percent composition
concepts.statement: When only the percentages are known, a 100-g sample is assumed, so that each element’s mass in grams is numerically its mass percentage, and the usual procedure follows.

concepts.name: Deriving a molecular formula
concepts.statement: An empirical formula gives only the relative numbers of atoms. Dividing the molecular or molar mass by the empirical formula mass gives the number of formula units in each molecule, and multiplying every subscript by that number gives the molecular formula.

forms.latex: \frac{\text{molecular or molar mass}}{\text{empirical formula mass}}=n\;\text{formula units/molecule}
forms.condition: both masses in amu, or both in g/mol
a compound whose empirical formula is A<sub>x</sub>B<sub>y</sub>, with n empirical formula units in each molecule

concepts.name: Empirical formula mass
concepts.statement: The empirical formula mass of a compound is the sum of the average atomic masses of all the atoms its empirical formula represents.

concepts.name: Solution components
concepts.statement: A solution is a homogeneous mixture, and it usually has one component, the solvent, present at a much greater concentration than the others, the solutes, which are dissolved in it. A solution in water is an aqueous solution, the kind this book meets most often.

concepts.name: Concentration
concepts.statement: The relative amount of a given component of a solution is its concentration, and the properties of a mixture depend on it, as the sweetness of a coffee depends on its sugar. A solution is called dilute or concentrated in words before any unit puts a number on it.

concepts.name: Molarity
concepts.statement: Molarity is the number of moles of solute in exactly 1 liter of solution, and it is the concentration unit of most of chemistry. The liter is of the whole solution, not of the solvent that was added.

forms.condition: the volume is that of the whole solution, not of the solvent
the volume in liters
the molarity of a solution, written in millimoles and milliliters to shorten a titration calculation

concepts.name: Calculating with molarity
concepts.statement: The definition of molarity links three quantities, so any one of the amount of solute, the volume of solution and the molarity follows from the other two, and a molar mass brings in the mass of solute as well. Keeping a guard digit, or working the calculation in one step, keeps the rounding error out of the answer.

concepts.name: Dilution
concepts.statement: Dilution lowers the concentration of a solution by adding solvent, and it leaves the amount of solute unchanged. It is how melting ice weakens iced tea and how a laboratory prepares a working solution from a concentrated stock.

concepts.name: Dilution equation
concepts.statement: Since n = ML and the amount of solute does not change on dilution, the product of concentration and volume is the same before and after. The relation works in any units of concentration and volume that cancel, so it is written C<sub>1</sub>V<sub>1</sub> = C<sub>2</sub>V<sub>2</sub>.

forms.condition: a solution diluted by adding solvent; any units of concentration and volume that cancel
a solution diluted by adding solvent, so the amount of solute is unchanged

concepts.name: Solvent
concepts.statement: The solvent is the component of a solution present at a concentration higher than that of the other components.

concepts.name: Solute
concepts.statement: A solute is a component of a solution present at a concentration less than that of the solvent.

concepts.name: Aqueous solution
concepts.statement: An aqueous solution is a solution for which water is the solvent.

concepts.name: Dissolved
concepts.statement: A solute is dissolved when its components are dispersed in a solvent.

concepts.name: Concentrated
concepts.statement: A concentrated solution is one containing solute at a relatively high concentration; the term is qualitative.

concepts.name: Dilute
concepts.statement: A dilute solution is one containing solute at a relatively low concentration; the term is qualitative.

concepts.name: Mass percentage
concepts.statement: The mass percentage of a component is the ratio of its mass to the mass of the solution, expressed as a percentage. It is the unit on the labels of consumer products, and it needs only that both masses be in the same unit.

forms.condition: both masses in the same unit

concepts.name: Volume percentage
concepts.statement: A liquid dissolved in a liquid is conveniently described by the ratio of the volume of solute to the volume of solution, expressed as a percentage, since liquid volumes are easily measured.

forms.condition: both volumes in the same unit

concepts.name: Mass-volume percent
concepts.statement: A mixed unit takes the mass of solute and the volume of solution, as physiological saline is 0.9 g of solute per 100 mL and blood sugar is reported in milligrams per deciliter. Such units are common in biochemical and medical settings.

concepts.name: Parts per million and parts per billion
concepts.statement: Very low concentrations are expressed as parts per million or parts per billion, the mass ratio multiplied by 10<sup>6</sup> or 10<sup>9</sup>, just as a percentage is a part per hundred. They are the units of trace contaminants in water.

concepts.name: Converting concentration units
concepts.statement: A solution’s density converts its volume to its mass, and a molar mass converts a mass of solute to moles, so a concentration given in one unit can be expressed in another, from a mass percentage to a mass of solute or to a molarity.

concepts.name: Parts per million
concepts.statement: Parts per million (ppm) is the ratio of solute-to-solution mass multiplied by 10⁶.

forms.condition: the mass-based definition

concepts.name: Parts per billion
concepts.statement: Parts per billion (ppb) is the ratio of solute-to-solution mass multiplied by 10⁹.

forms.condition: the mass-based definition

concepts.name: Bond angles and bond distances
concepts.statement: The shape of a molecule is described by the distances between its nuclei and the angles between its bonds. A bond angle is the angle between two bonds that share an atom, measured in degrees, and a bond distance is the distance between the nuclei of two bonded atoms, measured in ångstroms or picometers.

concepts.name: Valence shell electron-pair repulsion theory
concepts.statement: VSEPR theory predicts the shape of a molecule from one assumption. The regions of high electron density in the valence shell of the central atom, bonding pairs and lone pairs alike, repel one another and settle into the arrangement that puts them as far apart as possible. The theory considers electron-pair repulsions alone, although nuclear-nuclear repulsions and nuclear-electron attractions also shape the arrangement a molecule finally adopts.

concepts.name: Electron-pair geometries
concepts.statement: The electron-pair geometry is the arrangement around a central atom of all its regions of electron density, and there are only five: two regions are linear, three are trigonal planar, four are tetrahedral, five are trigonal bipyramidal and six are octahedral. A single, a double and a triple bond each count as one region.

concepts.name: Molecular structure is not electron-pair geometry
concepts.statement: The electron-pair geometry describes where all the regions of electron density are, bonds and lone pairs together; the molecular structure describes where the atoms are and says nothing about the lone pairs. The two are the same when the central atom carries no lone pair and they differ whenever it carries one, which is why methane is tetrahedral while ammonia, with the same four regions, is trigonal pyramidal and water is bent.

concepts.name: Order of electron-pair repulsions
concepts.statement: The ideal angles are only approximate, because the regions of electron density are not all the same size. A lone pair repels more strongly than a bonding pair, and it occupies more space than a triple bond, which occupies more than a double bond, which occupies more than a single bond. That order is what explains the small distortions from the ideal angles, and it is what decides which arrangement is chosen when more than one is possible.

forms.latex: \text{lone pair-lone pair}>\text{lone pair-bonding pair}>\text{bonding pair-bonding pair}

concepts.name: Axial and equatorial positions
concepts.statement: In the linear, trigonal planar and tetrahedral arrangements every terminal position is equivalent, so it does not matter which one a lone pair takes. A trigonal bipyramid has two kinds of position: an axial position surrounded by 90° angles and an equatorial position with more room because of its 120° angles. A lone pair always takes an equatorial position, and in an octahedron with two lone pairs the two sit 180° apart, which is what makes ClF3 T-shaped and XeF4 square planar.

concepts.name: Predicting electron-pair geometry and molecular structure
concepts.statement: To predict a molecular structure, write the Lewis structure and count the regions of electron density around the central atom. Read off the electron-pair geometry, and use the number of lone pairs to name the molecular structure. Where more than one arrangement is possible, choose the one that minimizes repulsion. For a molecule with no single central atom, treat each interior atom in turn, each with its own local geometry.

concepts.name: Bond dipole moment
concepts.statement: A polar covalent bond leaves one atom with a partial positive charge and the other with a partial negative charge. The bond dipole moment measures this separation of charge; it is the product of the magnitude of the partial charges and the distance between them. We draw it as a vector pointing from the less electronegative atom toward the more electronegative one, with a small plus sign at the positive end and a length proportional to the electronegativity difference.

concepts.name: Assessing the polarity of a molecule
concepts.statement: A molecule is polar only if it contains at least one polar bond and its bond moments, added as vectors in three dimensions, do not cancel. Geometry is therefore as much of the answer as electronegativity: carbon dioxide has two polar bonds pointing in opposite directions and is nonpolar, while water has the same two bonds bent toward one another and is polar. Molecules of high symmetry such as BF3, CH4, PF5 and SF6 are nonpolar for the same reason, and polar molecules are the ones that align in an electric field and dissolve readily in polar solvents.

concepts.name: Bond angle
concepts.statement: A bond angle is the angle between any two covalent bonds that share a common atom.

concepts.name: Linear
concepts.statement: A linear shape has two outside groups placed on opposite sides of a central atom, 180° apart.

concepts.name: Trigonal planar
concepts.statement: A trigonal planar shape has three outside groups placed in a flat triangle around a central atom, with 120° angles between them.

concepts.name: Tetrahedral
concepts.statement: A tetrahedral shape has four outside groups placed around a central atom at the corners of a tetrahedron, with 109.5° angles between them.

concepts.name: Trigonal bipyramidal
concepts.statement: A trigonal bipyramidal shape has five outside groups placed around a central atom: three form a flat triangle with 120° angles between them, and the other two lie above and below the plane, at 90° to it.

concepts.name: Octahedral
concepts.statement: An octahedral shape has six outside groups placed around a central atom at the corners of an octahedron, with 90° angles between adjacent groups.

concepts.name: Axial position
concepts.statement: An axial position is a location in a trigonal bipyramidal geometry with another atom at a 180° angle and the equatorial positions at 90° angles.

concepts.name: Equatorial position
concepts.statement: An equatorial position is one of the three positions in a trigonal bipyramidal geometry with 120° angles between them; the axial positions lie 90° from them.

concepts.name: Vector
concepts.statement: A vector is a quantity having both magnitude and direction.

concepts.name: Dipole moment
concepts.statement: The dipole moment of a molecule describes its separation of charge, determined by the vector sum of its individual bond moments, which depends on its molecular structure.

concepts.name: Polar molecule
concepts.statement: A polar molecule, or dipole, is a molecule with an overall dipole moment.

concepts.name: Writing a Lewis structure
concepts.statement: To write a Lewis structure, count the valence electrons of the molecule or ion, draw a skeleton with single bonds, complete the octets of the outer atoms with lone pairs, place the remaining electrons on the central atom, and form multiple bonds where the central atom still lacks an octet.

concepts.name: Polar covalent bonds and electronegativity
concepts.statement: When two bonded atoms differ in electronegativity, the shared electrons are pulled toward the more electronegative one, leaving it with a partial negative charge and its partner with a partial positive charge. The size of that difference sets the size of the bond's dipole moment.

concepts.name: Ionic lattice
concepts.statement: Because every compound is electrically neutral, the formula of an ionic compound gives the simplest ratio of ions whose charges cancel, as Al2O3 does with two Al3+ ions for every three O2− ions. The formula does not describe a molecule: the attraction between ions is the same in all directions, so each ion is drawn to all its neighbors of opposite charge and the ions build a three-dimensional lattice.

concepts.name: Predicting the charge of a monatomic ion
concepts.statement: A main group metal atom tends to lose all its valence electrons and a nonmetal atom tends to gain enough to fill its valence s and p orbitals, so in each case the ion takes the electron configuration of a noble gas and its charge can be read from the group. The heavy elements of groups 13 to 15 may also keep their valence s pair, the inert pair effect, which is why Tl+, Sn2+, Pb2+ and Bi3+ exist beside the expected ions.

concepts.name: Writing ion electron configurations
concepts.statement: The configuration of a cation is written by removing electrons from the neutral atom, and the configuration of an anion by adding them. For a transition metal the outermost s electrons are lost first, before any d electron, even though the d orbitals were the last to fill; so iron becomes Fe2+ by losing its 4s pair and Fe3+ by losing one 3d electron as well.

concepts.name: Inert pair effect
concepts.statement: Heavy atoms of groups 13 to 15 tend to form ions in which their valence s electrons are not lost, as in Tl⁺, Sn²⁺, Pb²⁺ and Bi³⁺.

concepts.name: Properties of ionic compounds
concepts.statement: The ionic bond is strong, which is why ionic solids are rigid and brittle with high melting points, and the ions are held in place, which is why the solid conducts poorly while the melt or the solution conducts well.

concepts.name: Covalent bond formation
concepts.statement: A covalent bond forms when two atoms share a pair of electrons that both nuclei attract. As two hydrogen atoms approach, the potential energy falls while each electron is drawn to both nuclei, and then it rises steeply as the nuclei repel. The bond length is the distance at which the energy is lowest. Breaking a bond always takes energy, and forming one always releases it.

concepts.name: Electronegativity and its periodic trend
concepts.statement: Electronegativity is the tendency of an atom to attract the electrons of a bond toward itself. On Pauling’s scale, it increases from left to right across a period and decreases down a group. The nonmetals of the upper right are therefore the most electronegative, fluorine above all at 4.0, and the group 1 metals are the least. Electronegativity is a calculated, dimensionless number; do not confuse it with electron affinity, a measured energy of an isolated atom.

concepts.name: Judging bond type by electronegativity
concepts.statement: The absolute difference in electronegativity between two bonded atoms is a rough measure of the bond's character: a small difference gives a pure covalent bond, an intermediate one a polar covalent bond, and a large one an ionic bond. It is only a guide, and the better one is the kind of atoms involved, since bonds between two nonmetals are generally covalent and bonds between a metal and a nonmetal are often ionic.

concepts.name: Bond length
concepts.statement: The bond length, or bond distance, is the distance between the nuclei of two bonded atoms at which the lowest potential energy is achieved.

concepts.name: Pure covalent bond
concepts.statement: A pure covalent bond, or nonpolar covalent bond, is a covalent bond between atoms of identical electronegativities.

concepts.name: Polar covalent bond
concepts.statement: A polar covalent bond is a covalent bond between atoms of different electronegativities, with a positive end and a negative end.

concepts.name: Writing Lewis symbols
concepts.statement: Write a Lewis symbol by surrounding the symbol of the element with one dot for each of its valence electrons. Remove dots to show a cation forming and add them to show an anion forming, so that the transfer of electrons in an ionic compound keeps the total number of electrons the same.

concepts.name: Octet rule
concepts.statement: Main group atoms tend to form enough bonds to have eight valence electrons around them, counting the shared electrons of each bond as belonging to both atoms. The number of bonds an atom forms can often be predicted from the number of electrons it needs to reach eight, so carbon forms four bonds, nitrogen three, oxygen two and fluorine one; hydrogen, which needs only two, is the exception.

concepts.name: Single, double, and triple bonds
concepts.statement: A single bond shares one pair of electrons between two atoms, a double bond shares two pairs and a triple bond shares three. Atoms share more than one pair when that is what it takes to give each of them an octet, as in formaldehyde and ethylene with their double bonds and carbon monoxide and the cyanide ion with their triple bonds.

concepts.name: Exceptions to the octet rule
concepts.statement: Three kinds of molecule cannot give every atom eight electrons. An odd-electron molecule, or free radical, such as NO, must leave one electron unpaired; an electron-deficient molecule such as BF3 has a central atom with fewer than eight; and a hypervalent molecule such as PCl5 or SF6 has a central atom of the third period or beyond that holds more than eight.

concepts.name: Lewis symbol
concepts.statement: A Lewis symbol is the symbol for an element or monatomic ion with a dot for each of its valence electrons.

concepts.name: Lewis structure
concepts.statement: A Lewis structure is a diagram showing the lone pairs and the bonding pairs of electrons in a molecule or an ion.

concepts.name: Lone pair
concepts.statement: A lone pair is a pair of valence electrons that is not used to form a covalent bond.

concepts.name: Single bond
concepts.statement: A single bond is a bond in which a single pair of electrons is shared between two atoms.

concepts.name: Double bond
concepts.statement: A double bond is a covalent bond in which two pairs of electrons are shared between two atoms.

concepts.name: Triple bond
concepts.statement: A triple bond is a covalent bond in which three pairs of electrons are shared between two atoms.

concepts.name: Free radical
concepts.statement: A free radical is a molecule that contains an odd number of electrons.

concepts.name: Hypervalent molecule
concepts.statement: A hypervalent molecule contains at least one main group element that has more than eight electrons in its valence shell.

concepts.name: Calculating formal charge
concepts.statement: Calculate the formal charge of an atom in a Lewis structure as the valence electrons of the free atom, less its lone pair electrons, less half its bonding electrons. The formal charges of a molecule add up to zero, and those of an ion add up to its charge.

concepts.name: Choosing a Lewis structure by formal charge
concepts.statement: When more than one Lewis structure can be written, the preferred one has formal charges of zero, or else the smallest nonzero formal charges, with adjacent formal charges zero or of opposite sign, and with any negative formal charge on the more electronegative atom. These guidelines explain why the least electronegative atom usually takes the central position.

concepts.name: Resonance forms and the resonance hybrid
concepts.statement: When two or more Lewis structures with the same arrangement of atoms can be written, none of them alone describes the molecule; the actual distribution of electrons is their average, the resonance hybrid. The molecule never switches between its resonance forms, which is why both N–O bonds of the nitrite ion and all three C–O bonds of the carbonate ion are found to be identical.

concepts.name: Formal charge
concepts.statement: The formal charge of an atom is the charge it would have if the electrons of each bond were shared equally: the number of valence electrons of the neutral atom, less its lone pair electrons, less half its bonding electrons.

forms.latex: \text{formal charge}=\text{\# valence shell electrons (free atom)}-\text{\# lone pair electrons}-\frac{1}{2}\,\text{\# bonding electrons}

concepts.name: Molecular structure
concepts.statement: The molecular structure of a molecule or ion is the arrangement of its atoms, without regard to its lone pairs.

concepts.name: Resonance forms
concepts.statement: Resonance forms are two or more Lewis structures that have the same arrangement of atoms but different arrangements of electrons.

concepts.name: Resonance hybrid
concepts.statement: The resonance hybrid is the average of the resonance forms shown by the individual Lewis structures, and it is the actual distribution of electrons in the molecule.

concepts.name: Bond energy
concepts.statement: The strength of a covalent bond is measured by its bond energy, the energy needed to break one mole of that bond in gaseous molecules, which for a diatomic molecule is the standard enthalpy change of its dissociation. In a molecule with several bonds of one kind the tabulated value is an average, since the first bond broken does not need the same energy as the rest.

forms.condition: a diatomic molecule XY in the gas phase

concepts.name: Bond strength and bond length
concepts.statement: The more electron pairs two atoms share, the stronger and the shorter their bond, so a triple bond is stronger and shorter than a double bond between the same atoms and a double bond is stronger and shorter than a single one. When one atom bonds to the members of a group, the bond grows weaker going down the group.

concepts.name: Estimating enthalpy from bond energies
concepts.statement: The enthalpy change of a reaction is approximately the energy needed to break every bond of the reactants less the energy released in forming every bond of the products. The estimate needs the Lewis structures of all the species, to know which bonds are single, double or triple, and it is rough because the bond energies are averages.

forms.condition: an estimate from average bond energies, for a reaction of gases

concepts.name: Lattice energy
concepts.statement: The lattice energy of an ionic compound is the energy needed to separate one mole of the solid into its gaseous ions, a positive quantity under the convention the book uses. It measures the strength of the attraction that holds an ionic solid together, and it is much larger than a covalent bond energy because it sums the interactions of every ion with the whole lattice.

concepts.name: Lattice energy trends
concepts.statement: Derived from Coulomb's law, the lattice energy is proportional to the product of the ionic charges and inversely proportional to the distance between the ions. Doubling both charges quadruples it, which is why MgO has nearly four times the lattice energy of LiF, and smaller ions give a larger lattice energy, which is why MgF2 exceeds MgI2.

forms.condition: an ionic crystal; C depends on the type of crystal structure

concepts.name: Using the Born-Haber cycle
concepts.statement: Lattice energies cannot be measured directly. The Born-Haber cycle breaks the formation of an ionic solid from its elements into steps whose enthalpies are known: sublimation of the metal, dissociation of the nonmetal, ionization of the metal atom, the electron affinity of the nonmetal atom, and the negative of the lattice energy. By Hess’s law, the steps add up to the enthalpy of formation, so any one of them can be found from the others.

concepts.name: Born-Haber cycle
concepts.statement: The Born-Haber cycle is a thermochemical cycle relating the energetic steps of forming an ionic solid from its elements: sublimation of the metal, dissociation of the nonmetal, ionization of the metal atom, the electron affinity of the nonmetal atom, and the formation of the lattice.

forms.condition: the formation of an ionic solid MX from a solid metal and a diatomic gaseous nonmetal, as for CsF

concepts.name: Valence bond theory
concepts.statement: Valence bond theory describes a covalent bond as the overlap of two half-filled atomic orbitals on different atoms, so that the single electrons in each orbital combine to form a pair shared between the two nuclei. The mutual attraction between this electron pair and the two positively charged nuclei is what holds the atoms together, and the strength of the bond depends on how much the orbitals overlap.

concepts.name: Bond distance and bond energy
concepts.statement: As two atoms approach, the energy of the system first falls, because each electron feels the attraction of the other nucleus, and then rises steeply, because the repulsions between the nuclei and between the electrons grow stronger than the attractions. The bond distance is the distance at which the energy is lowest, and the bond energy is the difference between that minimum and the energy of the separated atoms, which is the energy released when the bond forms and needed to break it.

concepts.name: Sigma and pi bonds
concepts.statement: A σ bond forms when orbitals overlap end to end along the internuclear axis, as two s orbitals, an s and a p orbital, or two p orbitals pointed at each other do. Its electron density is concentrated on the line between the nuclei. A π bond forms from the side-by-side overlap of two p orbitals. Its electron density lies on opposite sides of the internuclear axis, with a node along the axis itself. End-to-end overlap can be greater, so a π bond is generally weaker than a σ bond between the same two atoms.

concepts.name: Makeup of multiple bonds
concepts.statement: Between any two atoms the first bond formed is always a σ bond, and there can be only one σ bond in any one location. A single bond is therefore one σ bond, a double bond is one σ bond and one π bond, and a triple bond is one σ bond and two π bonds, which is why a carbon-carbon double bond is stronger than a single bond but not twice as strong.

concepts.name: Counting sigma and pi bonds
concepts.statement: Count the σ and π bonds of a molecule from its Lewis structure: every bond line contributes one σ bond, each double bond adds one π bond, and each triple bond adds two.

concepts.name: Overlap
concepts.statement: Overlap is the coexistence of orbitals from two different atoms in the same region of space, which leads to the formation of a covalent bond.

concepts.name: Sigma bond
concepts.statement: A sigma bond is a covalent bond formed by the overlap of atomic orbitals along the internuclear axis.

concepts.name: Pi bond
concepts.statement: A pi bond is a covalent bond formed by the side-by-side overlap of atomic orbitals, with its electron density on opposite sides of the internuclear axis and a node along the axis itself.

concepts.name: Hybridization of atomic orbitals
concepts.statement: Hybridization is a model of the changes in the atomic orbitals of an atom when it forms a covalent compound. It combines the wave functions of the atom's valence orbitals into a new set of hybrid orbitals whose directions match the observed geometry, as the 104.5° angle of water requires and unmodified 2p orbitals at 90° do not.

concepts.name: Properties of hybrid orbitals
concepts.statement: Hybrid orbitals exist only in covalently bonded atoms, they have shapes and orientations very different from those of the atomic orbitals they come from, and a set contains as many hybrid orbitals as atomic orbitals were combined to make it. All the orbitals of a set are equivalent in shape and energy, the kind of set depends on the atom's electron-pair geometry, and hybrid orbitals form σ bonds while unhybridized orbitals form π bonds.

concepts.name: sp, sp², and sp³ hybrid orbitals
concepts.statement: Mixing the valence s orbital with one p orbital gives two sp hybrids pointing 180° apart; with two p orbitals, three sp² hybrids at 120° in a plane, leaving one unhybridized p orbital perpendicular to it; with all three p orbitals, four sp³ hybrids pointing to the corners of a tetrahedron at 109.5°. Each hybrid holds a bonding pair or a lone pair, so the linear BeCl2, the trigonal planar BH3 and the tetrahedral CH4, NH3 and H2O are all described this way.

concepts.name: sp³d and sp³d² hybrid orbitals
concepts.statement: Five hybrid orbitals directed to the corners of a trigonal bipyramid need one d orbital as well as the s and three p orbitals, and six directed to the corners of an octahedron need two d orbitals. These hybridizations are possible only for atoms with d orbitals in their valence subshells, which rules out every atom of the first and second periods.

concepts.name: Drawing hybridization on an energy diagram
concepts.statement: Draw an orbital energy-level diagram with each orbital as a horizontal line at its energy and each electron as an arrow, setting the isolated atom beside the bonded one to show the valence electrons redistributed into the hybrid set. The diagram shows which hybrids are half filled and ready to pair with an electron from another atom, and which orbitals stay unhybridized.

concepts.name: Assigning hybridization
concepts.statement: The hybridization of an atom follows from the number of regions of electron density around it. Write the Lewis structure and count the regions, with single bonds, multiple bonds, radicals and lone pairs each counting as one. Then read the matching set from the table: two regions give sp, three sp², four sp³, five sp³d and six sp³d². VSEPR theory predicts the shape, and the hybrid orbitals explain how that shape forms.

concepts.name: Limits of hybridization
concepts.statement: Hybridization was devised to rationalize observed geometries, and it works well for small central atoms whose valence pairs are close together. For larger central atoms the pairs are farther from the nucleus and repel less, and the observed angles approach those of unhybridized p orbitals, so we invoke hybridization only where it is needed to explain the structure.

concepts.name: Hybrid orbital
concepts.statement: A hybrid orbital is an orbital created by combining atomic orbitals on a central atom.

concepts.name: sp hybrid orbital
concepts.statement: An sp hybrid orbital is one of a set of two orbitals with a linear arrangement that results from combining one s and one p orbital.

concepts.name: sp² hybrid orbital
concepts.statement: An sp² hybrid orbital is one of a set of three orbitals with a trigonal planar arrangement that results from combining one s and two p orbitals.

concepts.name: sp³ hybrid orbital
concepts.statement: An sp³ hybrid orbital is one of a set of four orbitals with a tetrahedral arrangement that results from combining one s and three p orbitals.

concepts.name: sp³d hybrid orbital
concepts.statement: An sp³d hybrid orbital is one of a set of five orbitals with a trigonal bipyramidal arrangement that results from combining one s, three p, and one d orbital.

concepts.name: sp³d² hybrid orbital
concepts.statement: An sp³d² hybrid orbital is one of a set of six orbitals with an octahedral arrangement that results from combining one s, three p, and two d orbitals.

concepts.name: Multiple bonds from unhybridized orbitals
concepts.statement: In a molecule with a double or a triple bond, the hybrid orbitals of each atom form the σ framework and the unhybridized p orbitals left over overlap side by side to form the π bonds. Each carbon of ethene uses three sp² hybrids for its σ bonds and one p orbital, perpendicular to the plane, for its π bond; each carbon of acetylene uses two sp hybrids for σ bonds and two perpendicular p orbitals for two π bonds.

concepts.name: Restricted rotation about a double bond
concepts.statement: Rotation about a single bond occurs easily, because the end-to-end overlap of a σ bond is symmetric about the internuclear axis and does not change as the atoms turn. Rotation about a double bond would twist the two p orbitals out of line and destroy their side-by-side overlap, essentially breaking the π bond, which is why all six atoms of ethene lie in one plane.

concepts.name: Resonance and hybridization
concepts.statement: Hybridization involves only σ bonds, lone pairs and single unpaired electrons, and resonance forms differ only in the arrangement of π bonds, which uses the unhybridized orbitals. Resonance therefore does not change the hybridization we assign, and either resonance form gives the same answer. The π electrons themselves are not located in one form or the other but are delocalized over the molecule, which valence bond theory does not easily describe.

concepts.name: Paramagnetism and diamagnetism
concepts.statement: A substance whose molecules have unpaired electrons is paramagnetic and is attracted into a magnetic field, while one whose electrons are all paired is diamagnetic and is weakly repelled; neither is a permanent magnet. Liquid oxygen collects between the poles of a magnet, which shows that the O2 molecule has two unpaired electrons although its Lewis structure pairs every electron.

concepts.name: Molecular orbital theory
concepts.statement: Molecular orbital theory describes the electrons of a molecule by molecular orbitals, formed by the linear combination of atomic orbitals, that extend over the whole molecule rather than belonging to one atom. Like an atomic orbital, a molecular orbital has a quantized energy and holds at most two electrons of opposite spin. The theory accounts for things valence bond theory cannot, among them the paramagnetism of oxygen and bonding described by several resonance forms.

concepts.name: Bonding and antibonding molecular orbitals
concepts.statement: Combining two atomic wave functions in phase is constructive interference and gives a bonding orbital, lower in energy than the atomic orbitals, with its electron density between the nuclei. Combining them out of phase is destructive interference and gives an antibonding orbital, higher in energy, with a node between the nuclei. Two atomic orbitals always give two molecular orbitals, one of each kind, and an asterisk marks the antibonding one.

concepts.name: σ and π molecular orbitals
concepts.statement: Molecular orbitals along the internuclear axis are σ orbitals, formed from s orbitals or from p orbitals overlapping end to end; those formed from p orbitals side by side, with electron density on opposite sides of the axis, are π orbitals. With the atoms on the x-axis, the six p orbitals of two atoms give σpx and σpx*, and two degenerate pairs of π and π* orbitals from the py and pz orbitals.

concepts.name: Filling a molecular orbital diagram
concepts.statement: A molecular orbital diagram sets the atomic orbitals of the two atoms at the sides and the molecular orbitals they form in the center, each as a line at its energy. Electrons fill it as they fill an atom: lower-energy orbitals first by the Aufbau principle, singly across degenerate orbitals before pairing by Hund's rule, two to an orbital with opposite spins. The filled diagram gives the molecular electron configuration, written with superscripts and with degenerate orbitals in parentheses.

concepts.name: Bond order
concepts.statement: In molecular orbital theory the bond order is the number of bonding electrons minus the number of antibonding electrons, divided by two, since a bond consists of two electrons. It usually agrees with the count of bonds in a Lewis structure, it is a guide to the strength of a bond between two given atoms, and a bond order of zero means that no stable bond forms.

forms.latex: \text{bond order}=\frac{(\text{number of bonding electrons})-(\text{number of antibonding electrons})}{2}

concepts.name: s-p mixing
concepts.statement: When the 2s and 2p orbitals of an atom are close in energy, the σs and σp wave functions combine, lowering the σs orbital and raising the σp orbital above the πp pair. The energy gap is small from lithium to nitrogen, so their diatomic molecules have the σp orbital above the π orbitals, and large for oxygen, fluorine and neon, whose diagrams keep the expected order. s-p mixing creates no new orbitals; it only shifts the energies of the existing ones.

concepts.name: Predicting diatomic configurations
concepts.statement: For a homonuclear diatomic molecule or ion of the first or second period, choose the diagram with or without s-p mixing, add or remove electrons for the charge, and fill it. Read off the configuration, the bond order and the number of unpaired electrons. The result predicts whether the species is stable and whether it is paramagnetic, and it explains the two unpaired electrons of O2 that the Lewis structure missed.

concepts.name: Paramagnetism
concepts.statement: Paramagnetism is the phenomenon in which a material that is not magnetic itself is attracted to a magnetic field. It occurs when the material contains unpaired electrons.

concepts.name: Diamagnetism
concepts.statement: Diamagnetism is the phenomenon in which a material that is not magnetic itself is repelled by a magnetic field. It occurs when all the electrons of the material are paired.

concepts.name: Molecular orbital
concepts.statement: A molecular orbital is a region of space in a molecule in which an electron has a high probability of being found. It extends over the whole molecule and holds at most two electrons of opposite spin.

concepts.name: Linear combination of atomic orbitals
concepts.statement: The linear combination of atomic orbitals is the technique of combining the wave functions of atomic orbitals, by adding or subtracting them, to create molecular orbitals.

concepts.name: Homonuclear diatomic molecule
concepts.statement: A homonuclear diatomic molecule is a molecule consisting of two identical atoms.

concepts.name: Bonding orbital
concepts.statement: A bonding orbital is a molecular orbital located between two nuclei. Electrons in a bonding orbital stabilize a molecule.

concepts.name: Antibonding orbital
concepts.statement: An antibonding orbital is a molecular orbital located outside the region between two nuclei, with a node between them. Electrons in an antibonding orbital destabilize a molecule.

concepts.name: σ bonding orbital
concepts.statement: A σ bonding orbital is a molecular orbital in which the electron density is found along the axis of the bond.

concepts.name: σ* antibonding orbital
concepts.statement: A σ* orbital is an antibonding molecular orbital formed by the out-of-phase overlap of atomic orbitals along the axis of the bond, which creates a node between the nuclei.

concepts.name: π bonding orbital
concepts.statement: A π bonding orbital is a molecular orbital formed by the side-by-side overlap of atomic orbitals, in which the electron density is found on opposite sides of the internuclear axis.

concepts.name: π* antibonding orbital
concepts.statement: A π* orbital is an antibonding molecular orbital formed by the out-of-phase side-by-side overlap of atomic orbitals, in which the electron density is found on opposite sides of the internuclear axis and there is a node between the nuclei.

concepts.name: Molecular orbital diagram
concepts.statement: A molecular orbital diagram is a visual representation of the relative energy levels of the molecular orbitals of a molecule, set between the atomic orbitals they are formed from.

concepts.name: Photon energy
concepts.statement: Light is absorbed and emitted in discrete packets called photons, and the energy of one photon is set by the frequency of the radiation, E = hν, or equivalently by its wavelength, E = hc/λ.

forms.condition: one photon of electromagnetic radiation

concepts.name: Line spectra
concepts.statement: A gas excited by heat or by an electric current emits light at a few sharp wavelengths rather than over an unbroken band, and each element shows its own set of lines. Classical electromagnetic theory predicts a continuous spectrum and cannot account for this.

concepts.name: Wave properties
concepts.statement: Every wave, electromagnetic radiation included, has a wavelength, the distance between two consecutive peaks or troughs; a frequency, the number of cycles that pass a point per unit time; and an amplitude, one-half the height from peak to trough. The amplitude is related to the intensity of the wave, which for light is its brightness. We describe light by its wavelength and frequency.

concepts.name: Wave speed
concepts.statement: The product of a wave's wavelength and its frequency is its speed, and for electromagnetic radiation in a vacuum that speed is the constant c. Wavelength and frequency are therefore inversely proportional: as one increases, the other decreases, and either one may be found from the other.

forms.condition: electromagnetic radiation in a vacuum

concepts.name: Electromagnetic spectrum
concepts.statement: Electromagnetic radiation spans an enormous range of wavelengths, from gamma rays and X-rays through ultraviolet, visible, and infrared light to microwaves and radio waves, and visible light makes up only a small portion of it. Across the spectrum the energy and frequency increase as the wavelength decreases, and each region is put to its own uses.

concepts.name: Standing waves and quantization
concepts.statement: A standing wave is confined to a region of space. A string held fixed at its two ends can form only waves with an integer number of half-wavelengths between them. This is an example of quantization, in which only discrete values of a property are observed. The points between the ends that do not move are nodes, and their number grows with the energy of the wave.

concepts.name: Blackbody radiation and Planck’s quantized energies
concepts.statement: A heated object gives off a continuous spectrum whose distribution depends only on its temperature, and the peak of the curve moves to shorter wavelengths as the temperature rises. Classical theory predicted an intensity that grows without limit at short wavelengths, the ultraviolet catastrophe; Planck fitted the observed curves by restricting the vibrational energies to discrete values, E = nhν, which was the first appearance of energy quantization.

forms.condition: the vibrating atoms of a blackbody, restricted to discrete energies for each frequency

concepts.name: Photoelectric effect
concepts.statement: Light ejects electrons from a clean metal surface only when its frequency is above a threshold, and the kinetic energy of the ejected electrons rises with the frequency and not with the brightness, while the number of electrons rises with the brightness. Einstein explained this by treating light as a stream of photons, each carrying the energy hν, so that only a photon with enough energy can free an electron.

concepts.name: Wave-particle duality
concepts.statement: Some behavior of light, such as the interference fringes it makes after passing through two narrow slits, can be explained only by waves. Other behavior, such as the photoelectric effect, can be explained only by particles. Light is both wavelike and particle-like, and this is called wave-particle duality. Matter shows the same duality.

concepts.name: Wave
concepts.statement: A wave is an oscillation of a property over time or space, and it can transport energy from one point to another.

concepts.name: Wavelength
concepts.statement: The wavelength of a wave is the distance between two consecutive peaks or troughs.

concepts.name: Frequency
concepts.statement: The frequency of a wave is the number of wave cycles, peaks or troughs, that pass a specified point in space per unit time.

concepts.name: Hertz
concepts.statement: The hertz is the unit of frequency, one cycle per second.

concepts.name: Amplitude
concepts.statement: The amplitude of a wave is the extent of the displacement it causes, one-half the height from peak to trough.

concepts.name: Intensity
concepts.statement: Intensity is the property of the energy a wave carries that is related to its amplitude, such as the brightness of light or the loudness of sound.

concepts.name: Electromagnetic radiation
concepts.statement: Electromagnetic radiation is energy transmitted by waves that have an electric-field component and a magnetic-field component.

concepts.name: Interference pattern
concepts.statement: An interference pattern is a pattern of alternating bright and dark fringes that results from the constructive and destructive interference of waves.

concepts.name: Standing wave
concepts.statement: A standing wave, or stationary wave, is a wave localized in a region of space, with discrete wavelengths determined by the boundaries of that region.

concepts.name: Node
concepts.statement: A node is any point of a standing wave with zero amplitude. In an orbital, a node is a place where the probability of finding the electron is zero.

concepts.name: Quantization
concepts.statement: Quantization is the limitation of some property to specific discrete values rather than a continuous range.

concepts.name: Blackbody
concepts.statement: A blackbody is an idealized perfect absorber of all incident electromagnetic radiation. When heated, it emits radiation in a characteristic continuous distribution of wavelengths.

concepts.name: Continuous spectrum
concepts.statement: A continuous spectrum is electromagnetic radiation given off in an unbroken series of wavelengths, as white light from the sun is.

concepts.name: Photon
concepts.statement: A photon is the smallest possible packet of electromagnetic radiation, a particle of light.

concepts.name: Rydberg equation
concepts.statement: The wavelengths of all the lines in the spectrum of hydrogen fit one empirical equation: one over the wavelength is the Rydberg constant times the difference of the reciprocal squares of two integers, n₁ less than n₂. Balmer's equation for the four visible lines is the case n₁ = 2.

forms.condition: every emission line of hydrogen, with n₁ and n₂ integers and n₁ < n₂
the four visible lines of hydrogen, as Balmer found them empirically

concepts.name: Instability of the planetary atom
concepts.statement: In the planetary picture the electron moves about the nucleus as a planet moves about the sun. An electron on such an orbit is always changing direction, and so is always accelerating, and classical electromagnetism says that an accelerating charge must continuously emit radiation. The orbit would then shrink until the electron spiraled into the nucleus, which would make every atom inherently unstable.

concepts.name: Bohr’s stationary states
concepts.statement: An electron in one of the allowed orbits of an atom does not radiate at all; it emits or absorbs radiation only when it moves from one allowed orbit to another. The energies of those orbits are quantized: the electron may possess certain discrete energies and no value between them.

concepts.name: Bohr energy levels
concepts.statement: The energy of an electron in the orbit labeled n is −k times the square of the nuclear charge, divided by the square of n. The constant k gathers the electron mass, the electron charge and Planck’s constant. The energies are negative because they are measured from E = 0, the ionization limit, where the electron has been removed from the nucleus altogether. They crowd toward zero as n grows, so the rungs of the ladder are far apart at the bottom and close together at the top. The energy needed to ionize a ground-state hydrogen atom is k itself.

forms.condition: a one-electron atom or ion of nuclear charge Z
hydrogen, for which the nuclear charge is +1
hydrogen in its ground state, the electron removed to an infinite distance

concepts.name: Ground state and excited state
concepts.statement: An atom whose electrons have the lowest energy possible is in its ground state, as a hydrogen atom is with its electron in the n = 1 orbit. Energy from outside can move the electron to an orbit with a higher n, and the atom is then in an excited state.

concepts.name: Emission and absorption of a photon
concepts.statement: When an electron moves between two allowed orbits, the atom emits or absorbs a single photon whose energy equals the difference between the two orbital energies. Falling to a lower orbit emits the photon, and absorbing one moves the electron up. Energy can be neither created nor destroyed, so the energy needed to lift an electron from one level to another equals the energy released when it returns. We use the absolute value of the difference because a frequency and a wavelength are always positive.

forms.condition: the electron moves between two allowed orbits, so that one photon carries the whole difference

concepts.name: Hydrogen-like atoms and ions
concepts.statement: Because Bohr's model follows one electron only, it applies just as well to He⁺, Li²⁺, Be³⁺ and the rest of the one-electron ions, which differ from hydrogen only in their nuclear charge. Helium, with two electrons, is already beyond the model, because it says nothing about how two electrons act on each other.

concepts.name: Bohr orbit radius
concepts.statement: The radii of the allowed orbits grow as the square of the quantum number and shrink as the nuclear charge rises. They are measured in units of the Bohr radius, the radius of hydrogen’s ground-state orbit. As the electron’s energy increases, it is found farther from the nucleus. The electrostatic attraction weakens with distance, so an electron farther out is held less tightly.

forms.condition: a one-electron atom or ion of nuclear charge Z

concepts.name: Rydberg constant from the Bohr model
concepts.statement: Putting the quantized energies of the Bohr model into the photon relation gives an expression for one over the wavelength that has the same form as the Rydberg equation, with the Rydberg constant equal to k divided by hc. Bohr’s theoretical value agreed excellently with the experimental one.

forms.condition: hydrogen, and the quotient k/hc is the Rydberg constant

concepts.name: Calculating transition energies
concepts.statement: Given the two quantum numbers and the nuclear charge, find the energy difference from kZ²(1/n₁² − 1/n₂²). Its sign tells you whether the photon is absorbed or emitted, and dividing hc by its magnitude gives the wavelength. The result can then be checked against a measured spectrum.

forms.condition: a one-electron atom or ion, the electron moving between the orbits n₁ and n₂
the hydrogen atom, the electron moving from the state n_i to the state n_f

concepts.name: Bohr’s model of the hydrogen atom
terms: Bohr's model of the hydrogen atom
concepts.statement: Bohr's model of the hydrogen atom is a structural model in which the electron moves around the nucleus only in circular orbits, each with a specific allowed radius and energy.

concepts.name: Quantum number
concepts.statement: A quantum number is a number having only specific allowed values, used to characterize the arrangement of electrons in an atom.

concepts.name: Ground state
concepts.statement: The ground state is the state in which the electrons in an atom, ion, or molecule have the lowest energy possible.

concepts.name: Excited state
concepts.statement: An excited state is a state having an energy greater than the ground-state energy.

concepts.name: De Broglie wavelength
concepts.statement: De Broglie extended wave-particle duality to matter: a particle of mass m moving with velocity v behaves as a wave whose wavelength is Planck's constant divided by its momentum. The wavelength of an electron in an atom is about the size of the atom, so its wavelike behavior is noticeable there, while that of a softball is far too small to detect. Viewed as a circular standing wave, an electron fits an orbit only when a whole number of its wavelengths fits the circumference, which explains Bohr's quantization.

forms.condition: a particle of mass m moving with velocity v
an electron viewed as a circular standing wave about the nucleus

concepts.name: Heisenberg uncertainty principle
concepts.statement: It is fundamentally impossible to determine simultaneously and exactly both the momentum and the position of a particle: the product of the two uncertainties is at least ħ/2. The limit is too small to notice for a baseball, but the mass of an electron is small enough that the uncertainty is large and significant, which is why an electron in an atom cannot be given a precise orbit.

forms.condition: a particle of mass m moving along x
an atom making a transition from one energy state to another

concepts.name: Wavefunctions and orbitals as probability
concepts.statement: Schrödinger described electrons as three-dimensional stationary waves, or wavefunctions ψ, and Born interpreted them: the electron is still a particle, and the square of the magnitude of ψ gives the probability of finding it near a point in space. An atomic orbital is the region in which an electron is most probable to reside, so the quantum mechanical model describes where the electron is likely to be rather than a path it follows.

forms.condition: the Schrödinger equation in its most general form

concepts.name: Principal quantum number
concepts.statement: The principal quantum number n = 1, 2, 3, … labels the energy levels of an electron in an atom and plays the role of the n of the Bohr atom. Orbitals with the same n form a shell. The greater n is, the farther the electron is from the nucleus and the greater its energy. A transition between levels absorbs or emits a photon that carries the energy difference.

concepts.name: Secondary quantum number
concepts.statement: The secondary (angular momentum) quantum number l takes the integer values 0 to n − 1 and specifies the shape of an orbital: l = 0, 1, 2, 3 are the s, p, d, and f orbitals, and orbitals with the same n and l form a subshell. An s orbital is spherical and a p orbital is dumbbell-shaped, and an orbital has n − l − 1 radial nodes, distances at which the probability of finding the electron is zero.

concepts.name: Magnetic quantum number
concepts.statement: The magnetic quantum number m_l takes the values −l to +l and specifies the orientation of an orbital in space, so a subshell holds 2l + 1 orbitals: one s, three p, five d, and seven f. Orbitals of the same subshell have the same energy and are called degenerate; in hydrogen all orbitals of one shell are degenerate, but in atoms with more than one electron the subshells of a shell differ in energy.

concepts.name: Spin quantum number
concepts.statement: Each electron has an intrinsic spin, a completely quantum property with no classical analogue, and it can be in only one of two states, m_s = +1/2 or −1/2. An electron acts as a tiny magnet, and in an external magnetic field the two spin states have slightly different energies, which is why some lines of the hydrogen spectrum are closely spaced pairs.

concepts.name: Pauli exclusion principle
concepts.statement: No two electrons in the same atom can have the same set of all four quantum numbers. Since the spin quantum number has only two values, an orbital can hold no more than two electrons, and two electrons in the same orbital must have opposite spins.

concepts.name: Working with quantum numbers
concepts.statement: Given a value of n, list the allowed values of l and m_l, name the subshells, and count the orbitals in each; a shell holds n² orbitals and at most 2n² electrons. Given a set of quantum numbers, name the subshell.

concepts.name: Velocity
concepts.statement: The velocity of a particle is the rate at which its position changes, the distance it travels per unit time in a given direction.

concepts.name: Momentum
concepts.statement: The linear momentum of a particle is the product of its mass and its velocity.

concepts.name: Quantum mechanics
concepts.statement: Quantum mechanics is the field of study that includes the quantization of energy, wave-particle duality, and the Heisenberg uncertainty principle to describe matter.

concepts.name: Wavefunction
concepts.statement: A wavefunction is the mathematical description of an atomic orbital. It describes the shape of the orbital, and it can be used to calculate the probability of finding the electron at any given location and the electron's energy.

concepts.name: Electron density
concepts.statement: Electron density is a measure of the probability of locating an electron in a particular region of space, equal to the squared magnitude of the wavefunction.

concepts.name: Atomic orbital
concepts.statement: An atomic orbital is the mathematical function, the wavefunction, that describes the behavior of an electron in an atom; it is pictured as the region of space in which the electron is most probably found.

concepts.name: Shell
concepts.statement: A shell is the set of atomic orbitals with the same principal quantum number, n.

concepts.name: Subshell
concepts.statement: A subshell is the set of atomic orbitals with the same values of n and l.

concepts.name: s orbital
concepts.statement: An s orbital is a spherical region of space with high electron density, the orbital with l = 0.

concepts.name: p orbital
concepts.statement: A p orbital is a dumbbell-shaped region of space with high electron density, an orbital with l = 1.

concepts.name: d orbital
concepts.statement: A d orbital is a region of space with high electron density that is either four-lobed or contains a dumbbell and a torus, an orbital with l = 2.

concepts.name: f orbital
concepts.statement: An f orbital is a multilobed region of space with high electron density, an orbital with l = 3.

concepts.name: Degenerate orbitals
concepts.statement: Degenerate orbitals are orbitals that have the same energy.

concepts.name: Energy order of atomic orbitals
