concepts.statement: In an atom with two or more electrons, the energy of the orbitals increases with n and, within a shell, in the order s < p < d < f, because electrons with larger l penetrate less toward the nucleus and are more shielded by the inner electrons. For larger atoms the two trends overlap, so that the 4s orbital lies below the 3d and the filling order runs 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d, 4p, and so on.

concepts.name: Aufbau principle
concepts.statement: The electron configurations of the elements are built by adding one proton to the nucleus and one electron at a time, each electron entering the subshell of lowest energy available, subject to the Pauli exclusion principle. Electrons enter higher-energy subshells only after the lower ones have been filled to capacity, and reading the periodic table in order of increasing Z gives the same order.

concepts.name: Hund’s rule
concepts.statement: The lowest-energy configuration of electrons in a set of degenerate orbitals is the one with the maximum number of unpaired electrons: each orbital of a subshell is singly occupied, with all spins alike, before any is doubly occupied. So the two 2p electrons of carbon sit in different p orbitals with the same spin.

concepts.name: Writing electron configurations and orbital diagrams
concepts.statement: An electron configuration lists each occupied subshell by its n, its letter, and a superscript that counts its electrons, as in 1s²2s²2p⁴. An orbital diagram draws each orbital as a box and each electron as an arrow. The inner electrons may be abbreviated by the symbol of the noble gas whose configuration they match, as in [Ne]3s¹ for sodium. You should be able to write either form for any atom and to identify an atom from its configuration.

concepts.name: Valence electrons and core electrons
concepts.statement: The electrons in the outermost shell are the valence electrons and those in the inner shells are the core electrons. Valence electrons have the highest energy, are the most easily lost or shared, and play the most important role in chemical reactions, and elements with the same number of valence electrons have similar chemical properties.

concepts.name: Exceptions to the predicted configurations
concepts.statement: Some atoms do not follow the predicted filling order because the subshells involved are very close in energy. Half-filled and completely filled subshells represent conditions of preferred stability, so chromium and copper each move an electron from 4s into 3d, and in niobium the repulsion of pairing two 5s electrons outweighs the small gap between 5s and 4d; there is no simple method to predict such exceptions.

concepts.name: Electron configurations and the periodic table
concepts.statement: The periodic table puts elements whose atoms have the same number of valence electrons in the same group, which is why the chemical properties recur periodically. The subshell that receives the last electron divides the table into the main group elements (s and p), the transition elements (d), and the inner transition elements (f), and this classification decides which orbitals are counted in the valence shell.

concepts.name: Electron configurations of ions
concepts.statement: A cation of a main group element loses the electrons that were added last. A transition or inner transition metal loses its highest ns electrons before its (n − 1)d or (n − 2)f electrons. An anion adds electrons in the order the Aufbau principle predicts. From these rules, write the configuration of an ion from that of its parent atom, or name an ion from a configuration and a charge.

concepts.name: Electron configuration
concepts.statement: An electron configuration is a listing that identifies the electron occupancy of an atom’s shells and subshells, as in 1s²2s²2p⁴.

concepts.name: Orbital diagram
concepts.statement: An orbital diagram is a pictorial representation of the electron configuration that shows each orbital as a box and each electron as an arrow.

concepts.name: Valence shell
concepts.statement: The valence shell of an atom is its high-energy outer shell or shells.

concepts.name: Valence electrons
concepts.statement: Valence electrons are the electrons in the high-energy outer shell or shells of an atom.

concepts.name: Core electrons
concepts.statement: Core electrons are the electrons of an atom that occupy the orbitals of its inner shells.

concepts.name: Effective nuclear charge
concepts.statement: The pull the nucleus exerts on one electron is its charge less the shielding of the other electrons. Core electrons shield well, while electrons in the same valence shell shield each other poorly, so each step to the right across a period raises Z by one but the shielding only slightly, and the effective nuclear charge increases across a period.

forms.condition: any atom but hydrogen, whose inner electrons partly shield the outer ones

concepts.name: Covalent radius trend
concepts.statement: The covalent radius, one-half the distance between the nuclei of two identical atoms joined by a covalent bond, increases down a group because each step adds a shell farther from the nucleus, and decreases from left to right across a period because the rising effective nuclear charge draws the electrons closer.

concepts.name: Ionic radius trend
concepts.statement: A cation is smaller than its parent atom, since the remaining electrons feel a greater effective nuclear charge, and a cation of higher charge is smaller still; an anion is larger than its parent, since the added electrons repel one another. Atoms and ions with the same electron configuration are isoelectronic, and among them the one with the greater nuclear charge is the smaller.

concepts.name: Ionization energy trend
concepts.statement: The first ionization energy, the energy required to remove the most loosely bound electron from a gaseous atom, is always positive and generally decreases down a group and increases across a period, the opposite of the trend in size. It dips each time a new subshell begins, as from beryllium to boron, and again where a p subshell becomes more than half-filled, as from nitrogen to oxygen.

concepts.name: Successive ionization energies
concepts.statement: Removing an electron from a cation is harder than removing one from a neutral atom, so the successive ionization energies of an element always increase. There is a large jump when the core electrons begin to be removed, which falls after the last valence electron: after the third ionization for scandium and gallium, for example.

forms.condition: the cation losing its second most loosely bound electron

concepts.name: Electron affinity trend
concepts.statement: The electron affinity is the energy change when a gaseous atom accepts an electron; it is negative when energy is released and positive otherwise. Electron affinities tend to become more negative across a period as the effective nuclear charge increases. Groups 2, 15 and 18 are exceptions, because a filled or half-filled subshell resists the added electron. The second element of a group, such as chlorine, often has a more negative value than the first, because the small n = 2 shell crowds its electrons.

concepts.name: Predicting periodic trends
concepts.statement: From the positions of elements in the periodic table, order atoms and ions by radius, ionization energy or electron affinity. Combine the trend down a group with the trend across a period, and allow for the known exceptions. Metallic character follows the same trend as size, so the same reading tells which elements lose electrons most easily.

concepts.name: Covalent radius
concepts.statement: The covalent radius of an atom is one-half the distance between the nuclei of two identical atoms when they are joined by a covalent bond.

concepts.name: Isoelectronic species
concepts.statement: Atoms or ions that have identical electron configurations are isoelectronic.

concepts.name: Ionization energy
concepts.statement: The ionization energy is the energy required to remove an electron from a gaseous atom or ion. The first ionization energy, IE₁, removes the most loosely bound electron of the neutral atom.

forms.condition: a gaseous atom in its ground state losing its most loosely bound electron

concepts.name: Electron affinity
concepts.statement: The electron affinity is the energy change associated with the addition of an electron to a gaseous atom or ion. It is negative when energy is released.

forms.condition: a gaseous atom accepting an electron to form an anion

concepts.name: Solutions and their defining traits
concepts.statement: A solution is a homogeneous mixture in which the solute particles are individually dispersed among the solvent’s, so its composition is uniform, its state is usually the solvent’s, and its solute never settles out. Almost any gas, liquid or solid can act as a solvent, so air and brass are solutions just as saltwater is.

concepts.name: Ideal solutions and matter dispersal
concepts.statement: When the attractions between unlike particles are no different from those between like particles, a solution forms with no change in energy, and it forms anyway, driven by the increased dispersal of matter alone.

concepts.name: Dissolution as three steps
concepts.statement: The formation of a solution may be viewed as separating the solute particles and the solvent particles, both endothermic, and then letting solute and solvent attract one another (solvation), which is exothermic. The balance of the three steps decides whether dissolving releases or absorbs heat.

concepts.name: Heat released or absorbed on dissolving
concepts.statement: A solute whose solvation releases more energy than its separation costs dissolves exothermically, as sodium hydroxide does; one whose separation costs more dissolves endothermically, as ammonium nitrate does, and it can still dissolve because of the increase in dispersal.

concepts.name: Predicting solution formation
concepts.statement: Naming the strongest attractions within the solute, within the solvent and between the two lets us predict whether they will mix and which solvent suits a solute.

concepts.name: Alloy
concepts.statement: An alloy is a solid mixture of a metallic element and one or more additional elements.

concepts.name: Spontaneous process
concepts.statement: A spontaneous process is a physical or chemical change that occurs without the addition of energy from an external source.

concepts.name: Solvation
concepts.statement: Solvation is the exothermic process in which intermolecular attractions between solute and solvent form as the solute particles are surrounded by solvent particles.

concepts.name: Electrolytes and nonelectrolytes
concepts.statement: An electrolyte yields ions when it dissolves, so its solution conducts electricity; a nonelectrolyte yields none. A strong electrolyte yields ions essentially completely, a weak electrolyte only in small part.

concepts.name: Ion-dipole attraction
concepts.statement: The electrostatic attraction between an ion and a polar molecule turns the negative oxygen ends of water molecules toward a cation and the positive hydrogen ends toward an anion, and it is what lets water pull ions out of a solid.

concepts.name: Ionic compounds dissociate
concepts.statement: When an ionic compound dissolves, water surrounds and solvates its ions and they disperse through the solution, a physical change called dissociation. Ionic compounds dissociate nearly completely, so even a sparingly soluble one is a strong electrolyte.

concepts.name: Covalent electrolytes react with water
concepts.statement: Some covalent compounds conduct once dissolved because their molecules react chemically with water to form ions: a strong acid such as HCl ionizes completely and is a strong electrolyte, while weak acids and bases ionize partly and are weak electrolytes.

concepts.name: Classifying electrolytes
concepts.statement: Whether a solute is ionic, a strong acid, a weak acid or base, or an unreactive covalent compound tells us how well its solution will conduct.

concepts.name: Electrolyte
concepts.statement: An electrolyte is a substance that produces ions when dissolved in water, so that its solution conducts electricity.

concepts.name: Nonelectrolyte
concepts.statement: A nonelectrolyte is a substance that does not produce ions when dissolved in water.

concepts.name: Strong electrolyte
concepts.statement: A strong electrolyte is a substance that dissociates or ionizes completely when dissolved in water.

concepts.name: Weak electrolyte
concepts.statement: A weak electrolyte is a substance that ionizes only partially when dissolved in water.

concepts.name: Solubility and saturation
concepts.statement: The solubility of a solute is the maximum concentration it can reach in a solvent under given conditions when dissolution is at equilibrium. A solution at that concentration is saturated, one below it is unsaturated.

concepts.name: Supersaturated solutions
concepts.statement: A solution can hold more solute than its solubility, a nonequilibrium state that ends in precipitation or loss of gas when it is disturbed. Cooling a saturated solution of a solid, or warming or depressurizing a solution of a gas, can prepare one.

concepts.name: Gas solubility and temperature
concepts.statement: Since a gaseous solute has no solute-solute attraction to overcome, only its attraction to the solvent sets its solubility, and that solubility typically decreases as the temperature increases, which is why thermal pollution starves natural waters of oxygen.

concepts.name: Henry’s law
concepts.statement: The quantity of an ideal gas that dissolves in a definite volume of liquid is directly proportional to the pressure of the gas, $C_{\text{g}} = kP_{\text{g}}$, with k set by the gas, the solvent and the temperature. A gas that reacts with the solvent, as ammonia does with water, dissolves more than the law predicts.

forms.condition: a gas that does not react with the solvent, at a fixed temperature

concepts.name: Using Henry’s law
concepts.statement: Finding k from one known solubility and pressure gives the solubility at any other pressure, and a constant read from a solubility graph answers whether a stream holds enough oxygen for its fish.

concepts.name: Miscibility
concepts.statement: Liquids of similar polarity mix in all proportions because the attractions between unlike molecules are as strong as those between like ones, an illustration of “like dissolves like”; a nonpolar liquid and water form separate layers, and some pairs are only partially miscible.

concepts.name: Solubility curves of solids
concepts.statement: The solubilities of most solids in water increase with temperature, though some, such as cerium sulfate, decrease, and a solubility curve reads off how much of a solid dissolves in 100 g of water at any temperature.

concepts.name: Saturated solution
concepts.statement: A saturated solution has a concentration equal to the solubility of its solute, the maximum concentration possible at that temperature and pressure.

concepts.name: Unsaturated solution
concepts.statement: An unsaturated solution has a concentration less than the solubility of its solute.

concepts.name: Miscible
concepts.statement: Liquids are miscible when they are mutually soluble in all proportions.

concepts.name: Immiscible
concepts.statement: Liquids are immiscible when their mutual solubility is negligible.

concepts.name: Partially miscible
concepts.statement: Liquids are partially miscible when they are of moderate mutual solubility.

concepts.name: Colligative properties
concepts.statement: Vapor pressure lowering, boiling point elevation, freezing point depression and osmotic pressure depend only on the total concentration of solute particles, not on their identity, mass or size.

concepts.name: Molality and mole fraction
concepts.statement: Because mole fraction and molality are built from masses and moles, either can be converted into the other, or into molarity or mass percentage, with the molar masses of the components and, for molarity, the density of the solution. Unlike molarity, neither changes with temperature.

concepts.name: Raoult’s law and vapor pressure lowering
concepts.statement: The partial pressure of a component of an ideal solution is its mole fraction times the vapor pressure of the pure component, so a nonvolatile solute lowers the vapor pressure of the solvent in proportion to how much it dilutes the solvent.

forms.condition: component A of an ideal solution
an ideal solution of i components
a solution whose solutes are all nonvolatile

concepts.name: Distillation
concepts.statement: The vapor above a mixture of two volatile liquids is richer in the more volatile one, so heating the mixture and condensing the vapor separates them; a fractionating column repeats the separation many times over.

concepts.name: Boiling point elevation
concepts.statement: Because a nonvolatile solute lowers the vapor pressure, the solution must be hotter than the pure solvent before its vapor pressure reaches the atmosphere’s, and the elevation is proportional to the molality of all solute species, $\Delta T_{\text{b}} = K_{\text{b}}m$.

forms.condition: a dilute solution of nonvolatile solute, m counting all solute species

concepts.name: Freezing point depression
concepts.statement: A solution freezes at a lower temperature than its pure solvent, by an amount proportional to the molality of all solute species, $\Delta T_{\text{f}} = K_{\text{f}}m$, because only the solvent freezes out; salted roads and antifreeze exploit it.

forms.condition: a dilute solution, m counting all solute species

concepts.name: Osmosis and osmotic pressure
concepts.statement: Solvent diffuses through a semipermeable membrane into a solution faster than it returns, until the solution’s rising pressure equalizes the rates; that pressure is the osmotic pressure, $\Pi = MRT$. Applying more pressure reverses osmosis, and a cell swells or shrivels in a hypotonic or hypertonic solution.

forms.condition: a dilute solution, with T in kelvin

concepts.name: Finding molar mass from a colligative property
concepts.statement: A measured freezing point depression, boiling point elevation or osmotic pressure gives the moles of solute in a known mass, and so the solute’s molar mass.

concepts.name: Van’t Hoff factor
concepts.statement: An electrolyte yields more than one particle per formula unit, so its colligative effects are multiplied by the van’t Hoff factor i, the moles of particles per mole of formula units; residual attraction between ions, even ion pairs, makes the measured i smaller than predicted.

forms.latex: i=\frac{\text{moles of particles in solution}}{\text{moles of formula units dissolved}}
forms.condition: a dissolved electrolyte or nonelectrolyte

concepts.name: Molality
concepts.statement: Molality is a concentration unit defined as the number of moles of solute divided by the mass of the solvent in kilograms. Since it is built from moles and masses, it does not change with temperature.

forms.condition: the molal concentration of a solute

concepts.name: Boiling point elevation constant
concepts.statement: The boiling point elevation constant, or ebullioscopic constant, of a solvent is the proportionality constant relating the boiling point elevation of its solutions to the molality of solute.

concepts.name: Freezing point depression constant
concepts.statement: The freezing point depression constant, or cryoscopic constant, of a solvent is the proportionality constant relating the freezing point depression of its solutions to the molality of solute.

concepts.name: Semipermeable membrane
concepts.statement: A semipermeable membrane is a membrane that selectively permits the passage of certain ions or molecules.

concepts.name: Osmosis
concepts.statement: Osmosis is the diffusion of solvent molecules through a semipermeable membrane.

concepts.name: Isotonic
concepts.statement: Two solutions are isotonic when they have equal osmotic pressures.

concepts.name: Hypertonic
concepts.statement: A solution is hypertonic to another when its osmotic pressure is greater.

concepts.name: Hypotonic
concepts.statement: A solution is hypotonic to another when its osmotic pressure is less.

concepts.name: Crenation
concepts.statement: Crenation is the shriveling of biological cells as they lose water by osmosis, as red blood cells do in a hypertonic solution.

concepts.name: Hemolysis
concepts.statement: Hemolysis is the rupture of red blood cells as they take up excess water by osmosis, as they do in a hypotonic solution.

concepts.name: Ion pair
concepts.statement: An ion pair is a solvated cation and anion held together by moderate electrostatic attraction, which lowers the number of independent particles in a solution of an electrolyte.

concepts.name: Colloids between solutions and suspensions
concepts.statement: A colloid’s particles are larger than most molecules yet small enough not to settle, so a colloid is intermediate between a solution, whose particles are molecules or ions, and a suspension, whose particles settle; colloidal particles scatter light, the Tyndall effect.

concepts.name: Dispersed phase and dispersion medium
concepts.statement: A colloid’s minor, particulate component is the dispersed phase and the substance it is spread through is the dispersion medium, and nearly every combination of states occurs: sols, aerosols, emulsions, foams and gels.

concepts.name: Preparing colloids and emulsions
concepts.statement: Colloidal particles are made by dispersion, grinding larger particles down, or by condensation, growing them from molecules or ions; an emulsion of two immiscible liquids is kept from separating by an emulsifying agent.

concepts.name: How soaps and detergents clean
concepts.statement: Soap and detergent molecules are amphiphilic, a nonpolar hydrocarbon end and an ionic end, so they gather at the boundary between grease and water and suspend the grease as colloidal particles that wash away.

concepts.name: Colloidal particles are charged
concepts.statement: The particles of one colloid carry charges of the same sign, which keeps them dispersed by repulsion, and highly charged electrodes attract, neutralize and deposit them, as in the Cottrell precipitator that cleans smoke.

concepts.name: Colloid
concepts.statement: A colloid, or colloidal dispersion, is a mixture in which relatively large solid or liquid particles are dispersed uniformly throughout a gas, liquid or solid and do not settle.

concepts.name: Suspension
concepts.statement: A suspension is a heterogeneous mixture in which relatively large particles are temporarily dispersed but settle out over time.

concepts.name: Tyndall effect
concepts.statement: The Tyndall effect is the scattering of visible light by a colloidal dispersion, which makes the path of a beam visible through it.

concepts.name: Dispersed phase
concepts.statement: The dispersed phase of a colloid is the substance present as relatively large solid or liquid particles.

concepts.name: Dispersion medium
concepts.statement: The dispersion medium of a colloid is the solid, liquid or gas in which the colloidal particles are dispersed.

concepts.name: Emulsion
concepts.statement: An emulsion is a colloid formed from immiscible liquids.

concepts.name: Gel
concepts.statement: A gel is a colloidal dispersion of a liquid in a solid.

concepts.name: Amphiphilic
concepts.statement: A molecule is amphiphilic when it has both a hydrophobic, nonpolar part and a hydrophilic, polar part.

concepts.name: Emulsifying agent
concepts.statement: An emulsifying agent is an amphiphilic substance used to stabilize the particles of an emulsion.

concepts.name: Gas pressure
concepts.statement: Pressure is the force exerted per unit area, P = F/A. A gas exerts pressure on the walls of its container because its molecules collide with those walls, so a small force on a small area can give a larger pressure than a large force spread over a large one.

forms.condition: pressure as the force exerted on a given area

concepts.name: Converting among units of pressure
concepts.statement: Pressures are reported in pascals, kilopascals, bar, pounds per square inch, atmospheres, torr and millimeters of mercury, depending on who measured them and why. Converting among these units with the relations of Table 9.1 is the first step of nearly every gas calculation, since the gas constant has to be used in units that match the pressure.

concepts.name: Atmospheric pressure and the barometer
concepts.statement: The weight of the column of air above an object presses on it, and at sea level this atmospheric pressure is about 1 atm. A barometer measures it by balancing it against a column of liquid in an inverted tube, and because mercury is about 13.6 times denser than water, a mercury column of about 760 mm does what a water column over 10 m tall would do.

concepts.name: Hydrostatic pressure
concepts.statement: The pressure exerted by a column of fluid because of gravity is the product of its height, its density and the acceleration due to gravity. It is why the height of a liquid column can stand for a pressure at all, and it lets us check that 760 mm of mercury does correspond to 101,325 Pa.

forms.condition: a column of fluid of height h and density ρ under gravity

concepts.name: Reading a manometer
concepts.statement: A manometer is a U-shaped tube of liquid connected to a gas. In a closed-end manometer the difference in liquid levels is the pressure of the gas itself; in an open-end manometer it is the difference between the gas pressure and the atmospheric pressure, added when the level is higher on the open side and subtracted when it is higher on the gas side.

concepts.name: Force
concepts.statement: A force is a push or a pull on an object. A gas pushes on the walls of its container with a force that comes from the collisions of its molecules with those walls.

concepts.name: Area
concepts.statement: The area of a surface is its extent, measured in square units such as square meters. A force spread over a larger area gives a smaller pressure.

concepts.name: Acceleration due to gravity
concepts.statement: The acceleration due to gravity is the rate at which the speed of a falling object increases near the surface of the earth, about 9.8 m/s². It turns the mass of a column of fluid into the weight that presses on what lies beneath it.

concepts.name: Pascal
concepts.statement: The pascal is the SI unit of pressure, a force of one newton on an area of one square meter: 1 Pa = 1 N/m².

concepts.name: Bar
concepts.statement: The bar is a unit of pressure equal to 100,000 Pa, close to the pressure of the atmosphere at sea level.

concepts.name: Atmosphere
concepts.statement: The standard atmosphere is a unit of pressure equal to 101,325 Pa, the average pressure of the atmosphere at sea level.

concepts.name: Torr
concepts.statement: The torr is a unit of pressure equal to 1/760 atm, almost exactly the pressure that supports a column of mercury 1 millimeter high.

concepts.name: Pounds per square inch
concepts.statement: Pounds per square inch is a unit of pressure common in the United States; 1 atm is 14.7 psi.

concepts.name: Barometer
concepts.statement: A barometer is a device used to measure atmospheric pressure, usually by the height of the column of liquid the atmosphere supports in an inverted tube.

concepts.name: Manometer
concepts.statement: A manometer is a device used to measure the pressure of a gas trapped in a container: a U-shaped tube of liquid whose difference in levels gives the pressure.

concepts.name: Amontons’s law
concepts.statement: The pressure of a given amount of gas is directly proportional to its temperature on the kelvin scale when the volume is held constant. This is the first of the four relationships the section establishes, and it is the one that explains why a sealed can warns against heat: the gas inside cannot expand, so everything the heating does shows up on the gauge.

forms.condition: a fixed amount of gas held at constant volume, with both temperatures on the kelvin scale

concepts.name: Charles’s law
concepts.statement: The volume of a given amount of gas is directly proportional to its temperature on the kelvin scale when the pressure is held constant. It is the law a balloon in a refrigerator demonstrates, and it is the one that makes a gas thermometer possible, since a volume read at a known pressure is a temperature.

forms.condition: a fixed amount of gas held at constant pressure, with both temperatures on the kelvin scale

concepts.name: Boyle’s law
concepts.statement: The volume of a given amount of gas held at constant temperature is inversely proportional to its pressure. Unlike the laws of Amontons and Charles, this is not a direct proportionality, and the graph of volume against pressure is a curve. Plotting the inverse of the pressure against the volume turns the same data into a straight line, which is easier to read.

forms.condition: a fixed amount of gas held at constant temperature

concepts.name: Avogadro’s law
concepts.statement: For a confined gas at constant pressure and temperature, the volume and the number of moles are directly proportional, which is another way of saying that equal volumes of all gases under the same conditions contain the same number of molecules. It is the law that makes the identity of the gas irrelevant, and it is what lets a volume stand in for a count in every gas calculation that follows.

forms.condition: a confined gas held at constant pressure and constant temperature

concepts.name: Absolute zero
concepts.statement: Both of the section’s direct proportionalities hold only when the temperature is read on the kelvin scale, and the reason is visible on their graphs: extrapolated to lower temperatures, the pressure line and the volume line both reach zero at –273 °C. That temperature is zero on the kelvin scale and the lowest there is, and it is why a gas law calculation in Celsius gives the wrong answer.

concepts.name: Ideal gas
concepts.statement: An ideal gas is a hypothetical construct whose properties are described exactly by the gas laws; no real gas is ideal. The ideal gas law can therefore be trusted only where real gases come close to ideal behavior, at relatively low pressures and high temperatures.

concepts.name: Ideal gas law
concepts.statement: Combining the four separate laws yields one equation relating the pressure, volume, amount and temperature of a gas, with the gas constant R carrying the units. It contains five terms, so specifying any four of them gives the fifth, and this single relation replaces the four laws for every calculation the rest of the chapter makes.

forms.condition: a gas behaving ideally, which is a good approximation at relatively low pressures and high temperatures
an ideal gas of molar concentration M

concepts.name: Combined gas law
concepts.statement: When the amount of gas is the same under two sets of conditions, PV/T equals the same product nR in both, so we can set the pressure, volume and temperature of the first condition equal to those of the second. Every two-state gas problem takes this form. Amontons’s, Charles’s and Boyle’s laws are the cases in which one of the three quantities does not change.

forms.condition: a fixed amount of an ideal gas under two different sets of conditions

concepts.name: Standard temperature and pressure
terms: standard conditions of temperature and pressure (STP)
concepts.statement: Standard conditions of temperature and pressure, STP, are 273.15 K (0 °C) and 1 atm (101.325 kPa), the conditions chemists agree to report the volume of a gas against. At STP one mole of any ideal gas occupies about 22.4 L.

concepts.name: Ideal gas constant
concepts.statement: The ideal gas constant R is the constant of proportionality in the ideal gas law, the same for every gas. Its value depends on the units of pressure and volume: 0.08206 L atm mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ or 8.314 L kPa mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.

concepts.name: Molar volume
concepts.statement: The molar volume of a gas is the volume occupied by 1 mole of it at a given temperature and pressure.

concepts.name: Standard molar volume
concepts.statement: The standard molar volume is the volume of 1 mole of gas at STP, about 22.4 L for any gas behaving ideally.

concepts.name: Gas density
concepts.statement: Substituting the ideal gas law into the definition of density shows that the density of a gas is its molar mass times its pressure divided by RT. Unlike the ideal gas law itself, this relation depends on the identity of the gas, so a density measured at a known temperature and pressure can identify a gas, and a heavier gas is denser than a lighter one under the same conditions.

forms.condition: an ideal gas of known identity

concepts.name: Finding the molar mass of a gas
concepts.statement: When a gas is unknown, measuring the mass, pressure, volume and temperature of a sample gives its molar mass through ℳ = mRT/PV. Compared with the mass of an empirical formula, that molar mass tells how many formula units make up a molecule, and the same measurement made on the vapor of a volatile liquid gives the liquid's molar mass.

forms.condition: a sample of an ideal gas of measured mass, pressure, volume and temperature

concepts.name: Dalton’s law of partial pressures
concepts.statement: Unless they react, the gases in a mixture do not affect one another’s pressure: each exerts the pressure it would exert alone in the container, and the total pressure of the mixture is the sum of these partial pressures. The partial pressure of each gas can therefore be found from the ideal gas law using its own amount.

forms.condition: a mixture of ideal gases that do not react with one another

concepts.name: Partial pressure from mole fraction
concepts.statement: The partial pressure of a gas in a mixture is its mole fraction times the total pressure. The relation lets us move between the composition of a mixture and the pressures of its components without computing each pressure from the ideal gas law.

forms.condition: a component A of a mixture of ideal gases

concepts.name: Finding the pressure of a gas collected over water
concepts.statement: A gas collected in an inverted bottle over water is saturated with water vapor, so the pressure it shows when the water levels are equal is the sum of its own partial pressure and the vapor pressure of water at that temperature. The pressure of the dry gas is the total pressure minus the vapor pressure of water, read from Table 9.2.

concepts.name: Combining volumes of gases
concepts.statement: Because equal volumes of ideal gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules, the volumes of gases that react or form are in the same ratio as the coefficients of the balanced equation. A volume of one gas can then be turned into the volume of another without passing through moles, provided both are measured under the same conditions.

concepts.name: Gas stoichiometry
concepts.statement: When a reaction involves a gas, the ideal gas law turns a measured volume, pressure and temperature into moles, and moles of gas back into a volume under any conditions. With the mole ratios of the balanced equation, this links the mass of a solid or liquid reactant to the volume of a gas produced or consumed.

concepts.name: Partial pressure
concepts.statement: The partial pressure of a gas in a mixture is the pressure that gas exerts, the pressure it would exert if it alone occupied the container.

concepts.name: Mole fraction
concepts.statement: The mole fraction of a component of a mixture is its amount in moles divided by the total amount of all the components, a concentration unit that carries no units of its own.

forms.condition: the mole fraction of a component A of a mixture

forms.latex: X_{\text{A}}=\frac{\text{mol A}}{\text{total mol of all components}}
forms.condition: any component A of a solution

concepts.name: Vapor pressure of water
concepts.statement: The vapor pressure of water is the pressure exerted by water vapor in equilibrium with liquid water in a closed container at a specific temperature. It rises with the temperature.

concepts.name: Mean free path
concepts.statement: The mean free path is the average distance a molecule travels between collisions. Gas molecules travel at hundreds of meters per second but collide billions of times a second, so the mean free path is short, and it grows as the pressure falls.

concepts.name: Diffusion and effusion
concepts.statement: Diffusion is the dispersal of molecules through space from regions of higher concentration to regions of lower concentration, which happens because the molecules move randomly and there are more of them to move away from a crowded region. Effusion is the escape of gas molecules through a tiny hole into a vacuum. The rates of the two processes differ, but for two gases the ratio of their rates is the same.

concepts.name: Graham’s law of effusion
concepts.statement: The rate of effusion of a gas is inversely proportional to the square root of its molar mass, so for two gases at the same temperature and pressure the ratio of their rates is the inverse ratio of the square roots of their molar masses. Lighter gases escape faster, which is why a helium balloon goes flat before an argon balloon does.

forms.latex: \frac{\text{rate of effusion of gas A}}{\text{rate of effusion of gas B}}=\frac{\sqrt{\mathcal{M}_B}}{\sqrt{\mathcal{M}_A}}
forms.ktex: \frac{\text{rate of effusion of gas A}}{\text{rate of effusion of gas B}}=\frac{\sqrt{\kMMB}}{\sqrt{\kMMA}}
forms.condition: two gases at the same temperature and pressure

concepts.name: Using Graham’s law
concepts.statement: Since the time for a given amount of gas to effuse is inversely proportional to its rate, the effusion times of two gases are in the direct ratio of the square roots of their molar masses. Graham’s law can then give an unknown effusion time, or a molar mass from a measured ratio of rates, which is a way of identifying a gas.

concepts.name: Diffusion
concepts.statement: Diffusion is the movement of atoms or molecules from a region of relatively high concentration to one of relatively low concentration, caused by their random motion.

concepts.name: Effusion
concepts.statement: Effusion is the escape of gaseous atoms or molecules from a container into a vacuum through very small openings.

concepts.name: Rate of diffusion
concepts.statement: The rate of diffusion is the amount of gas passing through a given area in a unit of time.

forms.latex: \text{rate of diffusion}=\frac{\text{amount of gas passing through an area}}{\text{unit of time}}
forms.condition: the definition of a rate of diffusion

concepts.name: Kinetic-molecular theory
concepts.statement: The kinetic-molecular theory explains the empirical gas laws with a microscopic model of five postulates: gas molecules move continuously in straight lines, they are negligibly small compared with the distances between them, their collisions with the walls cause the pressure, they exert no forces on one another so that their collisions are elastic, and their average kinetic energy is proportional to the kelvin temperature.

concepts.name: Gas laws from the kinetic-molecular theory
concepts.statement: Each gas law follows from the theory when pressure is read as the frequency and force of molecular collisions with the walls. Heating a gas at constant volume makes the collisions faster and more forceful, so the pressure rises; compressing it makes collisions with the smaller wall area more frequent; and adding molecules at constant pressure requires a larger volume to keep the collisions per unit area the same.

concepts.name: Distribution of molecular speeds
concepts.statement: The molecules of a gas move at widely varying speeds, but because there are so many of them the distribution of speeds is constant at a given temperature. It rises to a most probable speed and then falls off, shifts to higher speeds and flattens as the temperature rises, and lies at higher speeds for lighter molecules than for heavier ones at the same temperature.

concepts.name: Average kinetic energy and temperature
concepts.statement: The average kinetic energy of a mole of gas molecules is directly proportional to the kelvin temperature and does not depend on what the gas is. At a given temperature, then, all gases have the same average kinetic energy, and heavier molecules must move more slowly on average to have it.

forms.condition: a mole of an ideal gas, with R = 8.314 J/mol·K

concepts.name: Root mean square speed
concepts.statement: The root mean square speed is the square root of the average of the squared speeds of the molecules. Setting the two expressions for the average kinetic energy equal shows that it grows with the square root of the kelvin temperature and falls with the square root of the molar mass, which must be written in kilograms per mole.

forms.condition: an ideal gas, with the molar mass in kg/mol and R = 8.314 J/mol·K
a sample of n particles

concepts.name: Graham’s law from the kinetic-molecular theory
concepts.statement: The rate of effusion of a gas depends directly on the average speed of its molecules, and the root mean square speed is inversely proportional to the square root of the molar mass. The ratio of the effusion rates of two gases is therefore the inverse ratio of the square roots of their molar masses, which is Graham’s law obtained from the theory rather than from experiment.

concepts.name: Speed
concepts.statement: The speed of a particle is the distance it travels divided by the time it takes. The molecules of a gas move at a wide range of speeds.

concepts.name: Compressibility factor
concepts.statement: The compressibility factor is the ratio of the measured molar volume of a gas to the molar volume of an ideal gas at the same temperature and pressure, (PV_m/RT) measured. It equals 1 for an ideal gas, so its departure from 1 measures how far a real gas departs from the ideal gas law.

forms.latex: Z=\frac{\text{molar volume of gas at same }T\text{ and }P}{\text{molar volume of ideal gas at same }T\text{ and }P}=\left(\frac{PV_m}{RT}\right)_{\text{measured}}
forms.ktex: Z=\frac{\text{molar volume of gas at same }T\text{ and }P}{\text{molar volume of ideal gas at same }T\text{ and }P}=\left(\frac{\kP\kVm}{R\kT}\right)_{\text{measured}}
forms.condition: a real gas compared with an ideal gas at the same temperature and pressure

concepts.name: Non-ideal behavior
concepts.statement: Real gas molecules occupy some volume and attract one another. At high pressures the volume of the molecules themselves becomes an appreciable part of the whole, so the gas is less compressible than an ideal gas; at moderate pressures and low temperatures the attractions pull the molecules together, lowering the pressure at constant volume or the volume at constant pressure.

concepts.name: When a gas behaves ideally
concepts.statement: The ideal gas law describes a gas well when intermolecular attractions are negligible and the molecules occupy a negligible part of the volume, which is the case at low pressure and high temperature. It is this, and not a property of any particular gas, that justifies treating gases as ideal in most of the chapter’s calculations.

concepts.name: Van der Waals equation
concepts.statement: The van der Waals equation corrects the ideal gas law with two constants of each gas: a, for the attraction between molecules, adds n²a/V² to the pressure, and b, for the size of the molecules, subtracts nb from the volume. When the volume is large and the amount small, both corrections vanish and the equation reduces to PV = nRT.

forms.condition: a real gas, with the constants a and b of that gas

concepts.name: Reaction rate
concepts.statement: The rate of a reaction is the change in the amount or concentration of a reactant or product per unit time. Since a reactant’s concentration falls as the reaction proceeds, its change is multiplied by −1 so that the rate is, by convention, a positive quantity.

concepts.name: Average, instantaneous, and initial rates
concepts.statement: A rate computed over a time interval is an average rate; the rate at one instant is the instantaneous rate, the slope of the tangent to the concentration curve at that time, and the instantaneous rate at time zero is the initial rate. Like a car slowing toward a stop sign, a reaction’s average rate falls between its initial and final rates.

concepts.name: Calculating an average rate
concepts.statement: Dividing the change in concentration by the time interval over which it occurred, and changing the sign for a reactant, gives the average rate over that interval.

concepts.name: Relative reaction rates
concepts.statement: For aA ⟶ bB, the rate may be written from either species, and the two expressions agree once each change is divided by its coefficient: $\text{rate}=-\frac{1}{a}\frac{\Delta[\text{A}]}{\Delta t}=\frac{1}{b}\frac{\Delta[\text{B}]}{\Delta t}$.

forms.condition: the reaction aA ⟶ bB

concepts.name: Writing related rate expressions
concepts.statement: From a balanced equation, the rates of consumption of reactants and formation of products may be written as equal once each is divided by its coefficient, so a rate measured for one species gives the rate for every other.

concepts.name: Average rate
concepts.statement: The average rate of a reaction is the change in the amount or concentration of a reactant or product divided by the time interval over which it was measured.

concepts.name: Instantaneous rate
concepts.statement: The instantaneous rate of a reaction is its rate at one instant, the slope of the line tangent to the graph of concentration against time at that instant.

concepts.name: Initial rate
concepts.statement: The initial rate of a reaction is its instantaneous rate at t = 0 s, immediately after the reaction has begun.

concepts.name: Rate expression
concepts.statement: A rate expression is a mathematical representation that defines the rate of a reaction as the change in the amount, concentration or pressure of a reactant or product per unit time.

concepts.name: Chemical nature and rate
concepts.statement: Reactions that appear similar may proceed at very different rates under the same conditions, depending on the identity of the reactants.

concepts.name: Subdivision and rate
concepts.statement: A reaction between reactants in different phases takes place only at the interface between them, so a finely divided solid, with its greater surface area, reacts faster than one large piece.

concepts.name: Higher temperatures speed reactions
concepts.statement: Chemical reactions typically occur faster at higher temperatures, and for many processes the rate roughly doubles when the temperature is raised by 10 °C.

concepts.name: Higher concentrations usually speed reactions
concepts.statement: The rates of many reactions increase when the concentration of one or more reactants increases.

concepts.name: Catalyst
concepts.statement: A catalyst is a substance that increases the rate of a reaction without itself being consumed by the reaction.

concepts.name: Rate law
concepts.statement: A rate law relates the rate of a reaction to the concentrations of its reactants, each raised to a power called its order, multiplied by a rate constant. The concentration of a reactant whose order is zero does not appear, since any number raised to the zero power is 1.

forms.condition: the reaction aA + bB ⟶ products, with orders m and n found by experiment

concepts.name: Reaction orders and the overall order
concepts.statement: The exponent of a reactant’s concentration in the rate law is the order with respect to that reactant, and the overall order is the sum of these orders. Orders are usually 0, 1 or 2, but they may be fractional or negative.

concepts.name: Rate constant
concepts.statement: The rate constant k is specific to a particular reaction at a particular temperature; it does not depend on the reactant concentrations, but it does vary with temperature.

concepts.name: Rate laws are experimental
concepts.statement: The orders in a rate law must be found by observing how the rate changes with concentration; they sometimes match the coefficients of the balanced equation, but only by coincidence.

concepts.name: Finding a rate law by initial rates
concepts.statement: Comparing initial rates from trials in which one reactant’s concentration changes while the others are held fixed gives each order, from the ratio of rates or by logarithms; one trial’s data then give the rate constant.

concepts.name: Units of a rate constant
concepts.statement: The unit of k is whatever makes the rate come out in mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹, so it depends on the overall order x as L^(x−1) mol^(1−x) s⁻¹.

concepts.name: Predicting a rate from a rate law
concepts.statement: With a rate law and its rate constant, the rate at any set of concentrations may be calculated, and the effect of changing one concentration follows from its order.

concepts.name: Overall reaction order
concepts.statement: The overall reaction order is the sum of the reaction orders of all the substances that appear in the rate law.

concepts.name: Method of initial rates
concepts.statement: The method of initial rates is a common experimental approach to determining a rate law: the initial rate of a reaction is measured in trials with varying initial concentrations of its reactants.

concepts.name: Integrated rate laws
concepts.statement: Integrating a differential rate law gives an equation relating the concentration of a reactant to the elapsed time, which tells how much reactant remains after a period or how long a reaction takes to reach a given extent.

concepts.name: First-order integrated rate law
concepts.statement: For rate = k[A], the concentration falls exponentially, $[\text{A}]_{t}=[\text{A}]_{0}e^{-kt}$, so $\ln[\text{A}]_{t}=-kt+\ln[\text{A}]_{0}$ and a plot of ln[A] against t is a straight line of slope −k.

forms.condition: a reaction first order in A
a reaction first order in A

concepts.name: Second-order integrated rate law
concepts.statement: For rate = k[A]², $\frac{1}{[\text{A}]_{t}}=kt+\frac{1}{[\text{A}]_{0}}$, so a plot of 1/[A] against t is a straight line of slope k.

forms.condition: a reaction second order in a single reactant A

concepts.name: Zero-order integrated rate law
concepts.statement: For rate = k, the concentration falls linearly, $[\text{A}]_{t}=-kt+[\text{A}]_{0}$, and a plot of [A] against t is a straight line of slope −k. Zero-order behavior is seen only under certain conditions.

forms.condition: a zero-order reaction, under the conditions where it is zero order

concepts.name: Finding order from a linear plot
concepts.statement: Plotting [A], ln[A] and 1/[A] against time shows which is a straight line, which gives the order; the rate constant is then the slope or its negative.

concepts.name: Half-life
concepts.statement: The half-life is the time required for one-half of a given amount of reactant to be consumed; in each succeeding half-life, half of the remaining reactant is consumed.

concepts.name: Half-life by reaction order
concepts.statement: The half-life of a first-order reaction, $t_{1/2}=0.693/k$, is independent of concentration; that of a second-order reaction, $1/k[\text{A}]_{0}$, grows as the reactant is used up, and that of a zero-order reaction, $[\text{A}]_{0}/2k$, shrinks.

forms.condition: a first-order reaction
a second-order reaction
a zero-order reaction

concepts.name: Calculating with integrated rate laws
concepts.statement: Choosing the integrated rate law of the reaction’s order and solving it for the unknown gives the concentration remaining after a time, the time to reach a concentration, or the half-life.

concepts.name: Collision theory
concepts.statement: Reactant species must collide in order to react, so the rate of a reaction is proportional to the rate of collisions, and a collision leads to reaction only when it has a suitable orientation and enough energy. More molecules per unit volume mean more collisions, which is why rates rise with concentration.

concepts.name: Collision orientation
concepts.statement: The colliding species must meet in an orientation that brings together the atoms that will bond in the product.

concepts.name: Activation energy and the transition state
concepts.statement: The activation energy is the minimum energy a collision needs to form products; a collision with enough energy and the proper orientation forms an unstable, short-lived activated complex, or transition state. A reaction is slow when its activation energy is much larger than the average kinetic energy of the molecules.

concepts.name: Reading a reaction diagram
concepts.statement: A reaction diagram traces the energy of a system from reactants through the transition state to products; the activation energy is the height of the peak above the reactants, and ΔH is the difference between products and reactants.

concepts.name: Fraction of molecules with enough energy
concepts.statement: Of the molecules’ distribution of energies, only those above the activation energy can react; a lower activation energy or a higher temperature increases that fraction and so the rate.

concepts.name: Arrhenius equation
concepts.statement: The rate constant depends on the frequency factor A, which reflects how often molecules collide in a favorable orientation, and on the exponential term, which is the effect of the activation energy and the temperature.

forms.condition: a reaction whose kinetics follow the Arrhenius equation, T in kelvin
rate constants measured at several temperatures

concepts.name: Finding an activation energy
concepts.statement: A plot of ln k against 1/T is a straight line of slope −E_a/R, and rate constants at just two temperatures give E_a through the two-point form of the Arrhenius equation.

forms.condition: rate constants k₁ and k₂ measured at two temperatures T₁ and T₂

concepts.name: Activated complex
concepts.statement: An activated complex, or transition state, is the unstable combination of reactant species formed during a reaction at the highest energy along its path.

concepts.name: Frequency factor
concepts.statement: The frequency factor is the proportionality constant in the Arrhenius equation, related to the relative number of collisions that have an orientation capable of leading to product formation.

concepts.name: Reaction diagram
concepts.statement: A reaction diagram is a graph used in chemical kinetics to show how the energy of a reacting system changes as the reaction proceeds from reactants to products.

concepts.name: Reaction mechanism
concepts.statement: A reaction mechanism is the step-by-step sequence of elementary reactions by which a reaction occurs; the steps sum to the overall equation, and an intermediate is produced in one step and consumed in a later one.

concepts.name: Molecularity
concepts.statement: The molecularity of an elementary reaction is the number of reactant entities in it; termolecular steps are uncommon because three particles rarely collide at once.

concepts.name: Rate law of an elementary reaction
concepts.statement: Since an elementary reaction occurs exactly as written, its rate law may be written from its equation: first order for a unimolecular step, rate = k[A][B] or k[A]² for a bimolecular one.

concepts.name: Rate-determining step
concepts.statement: A reaction cannot proceed faster than its slowest step, so that step limits the overall rate; when it is the first step, the overall rate law is its rate law.

concepts.name: Testing a mechanism
concepts.statement: A rate law is determined by experiment and a mechanism deduced from it; a mechanism whose predicted rate law disagrees with the measured one is incorrect, and one that agrees is plausible.

concepts.name: Deriving a rate law from a mechanism
concepts.statement: The rate law of the rate-determining step is the overall rate law; when it contains an intermediate, a fast, reversible earlier step at equilibrium expresses the intermediate’s concentration in terms of the reactants.

concepts.name: Elementary reaction
concepts.statement: An elementary reaction is a reaction that takes place in a single step, precisely as depicted in its chemical equation.

concepts.name: Intermediate
concepts.statement: An intermediate is a species produced in one step of a reaction mechanism and consumed in a later step.

concepts.name: Unimolecular reaction
concepts.statement: A unimolecular reaction is an elementary reaction involving a single reactant entity.

concepts.name: Bimolecular reaction
concepts.statement: A bimolecular reaction is an elementary reaction involving two reactant entities.

concepts.name: Termolecular reaction
concepts.statement: A termolecular reaction is an elementary reaction involving three reactant entities.

concepts.name: Catalysis and activation energy
concepts.statement: A catalyst speeds a reaction by providing a different mechanism whose rate-determining step has a lower activation energy; it takes part in the reaction but is regenerated, so the overall reaction and the energies of reactants and products are unchanged.

concepts.name: Identifying a catalyzed path
concepts.statement: Of two reaction diagrams for the same reaction, the one with the lower activation energy for its rate-determining step is the catalyzed one.

concepts.name: Homogeneous catalysts
concepts.statement: A homogeneous catalyst is in the same phase as the reactants; it forms an intermediate that reacts further to give product and regenerate the catalyst.

concepts.name: Heterogeneous catalysts
concepts.statement: A heterogeneous catalyst is in a different phase, usually a solid, and furnishes a surface on which reactants are adsorbed, activated and react before the products desorb.

concepts.name: Enzymes as biological catalysts
concepts.statement: Enzymes are usually proteins that catalyze specific reactions of cellular metabolism by binding a substrate at an active site, in the lock-and-key or the induced fit model.

concepts.name: Reversible reactions
concepts.statement: A reversible reaction may proceed in both the forward (left to right) and reverse (right to left) directions, and a special double arrow is used in its equation to emphasize this.

concepts.name: Chemical equilibrium
concepts.statement: As a reversible reaction proceeds, the falling reactant concentration slows the forward reaction and the rising product concentration speeds the reverse reaction. When the two rates become equal, the concentrations of reactants and products remain constant and the system is at equilibrium.

forms.condition: a reversible reaction at equilibrium

concepts.name: Equilibria are dynamic
concepts.statement: A reaction at equilibrium has not stopped; it is proceeding in the forward and reverse directions at the same rate. Physical changes such as phase transitions establish such equilibria too, and the concentrations at equilibrium need not be equal, only constant.

concepts.name: Reaction quotient
concepts.statement: The reaction quotient, $Q$, is the product of the product concentrations, each raised to the power of its coefficient in the balanced equation, divided by the product of the reactant concentrations raised to theirs. Its value changes as the reaction proceeds, so it serves as an indicator of the reaction’s status.

forms.condition: the reaction mA + nB ⇌ xC + yD
the gas-phase reaction mA + nB ⇌ xC + yD

concepts.name: Writing reaction quotient expressions
concepts.statement: From a balanced equation we can write $Q_{c}$ using molar concentrations or, for gases, $Q_{P}$ using partial pressures, including terms only for gaseous and solute species.

concepts.name: Equilibrium constant
concepts.statement: The equilibrium constant, $K$, is the constant value of the reaction quotient exhibited by a system at equilibrium; $K_{c}$ is written with molar concentrations and $K_{P}$ with partial pressures.

forms.condition: a system at equilibrium; likewise K_P = Q_P

concepts.name: Magnitude of the equilibrium constant
concepts.statement: A reaction with a large $K$ reaches equilibrium when most of the reactant has become product, whereas a small $K$ means very little reactant has reacted. The magnitude of $K$ says nothing about how rapidly the reaction reaches equilibrium.

concepts.name: Predicting the direction of reaction
concepts.statement: A reaction proceeds in whatever direction is necessary to achieve equilibrium: forward when $Q < K$, in reverse when $Q > K$, and not at all when $Q = K$.

concepts.name: Relating Kp and Kc
concepts.statement: Since the partial pressure of an ideal gas is $P = MRT$, each pressure in $K_{P}$ is a concentration times $RT$, and the factors collect into $(RT)^{\Delta n}$, where $\Delta n$ is the difference in the molar amounts of product and reactant gases.

forms.condition: a gas-phase equilibrium, with Δn = (c + d) − (a + b) for aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD
the gas-phase reaction aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD

concepts.name: Homogeneous and heterogeneous equilibria
concepts.statement: In a homogeneous equilibrium all reactants and products are in the same phase; in a heterogeneous equilibrium they occupy two or more phases. Because the relative concentrations of pure liquids and solids equal 1, they do not appear in $Q$ or $K$.

concepts.name: Equilibrium constants of coupled equilibria
concepts.statement: Reversing an equation inverts its $K$, multiplying its coefficients by $x$ raises $K$ to the power $x$, and adding equations multiplies their $K$ values, so the $K$ of a net reaction follows from the $K$ values of the reactions that sum to it.

forms.condition: the equation written in the reverse direction
the coefficients of the equation multiplied by x
the net equation formed by adding two equations

concepts.name: Law of mass action
concepts.statement: At a given temperature, the reaction quotient for a system at equilibrium is constant, whatever the initial concentrations from which equilibrium was approached.

concepts.name: Homogeneous equilibrium
concepts.statement: A homogeneous equilibrium is one in which all reactants and products, and any catalysts, are present in the same phase.

concepts.name: Heterogeneous equilibrium
concepts.statement: A heterogeneous equilibrium involves reactants and products in two or more different phases.

concepts.name: Coupled equilibria
concepts.statement: Coupled equilibria are two or more equilibrium reactions that have in common one or more reactant or product species.

concepts.name: Le Châtelier’s principle
concepts.statement: A change in conditions that affects the forward and reverse rates differently (a stress) leaves the rates unequal, and the system experiences a net reaction in the direction of greater rate (a shift) that re-establishes equilibrium.

concepts.name: Concentration changes and equilibrium
concepts.statement: Adding reactant or removing product makes $Q_{c} < K_{c}$ and the equilibrium shifts right; removing reactant or adding product makes $Q_{c} > K_{c}$ and it shifts left. The new composition differs, but the value of the equilibrium constant is the same after the stress as before.

concepts.name: Volume changes and equilibrium
concepts.statement: Changing the volume changes every partial pressure by the same factor. If the reactant and product gases have equal total molar amounts, $Q_{P}$ is unchanged and there is no shift; otherwise decreasing the volume shifts the equilibrium toward the side with fewer moles of gas.

concepts.name: Temperature changes and equilibrium
concepts.statement: For an elementary reaction $K_{c}=k_{f}/k_{r}$, and the rate constants vary with temperature, so $K$ varies too. Treating heat as a reactant of an endothermic reaction and a product of an exothermic one predicts the shift: heating shifts an endothermic equilibrium right and an exothermic one left.

forms.condition: the elementary reaction A ⇌ B at equilibrium

concepts.name: Catalysts and equilibrium
concepts.statement: A catalyst lowers the activation energies of both the forward and the reverse reactions, so both are accelerated and equilibrium is reached more quickly, but without a change in the equilibrium constant.

concepts.name: Predicting an equilibrium shift
concepts.statement: Given a stress (a species added or removed, a change in volume or temperature, a catalyst), Le Châtelier’s principle predicts the direction of the shift and how each concentration changes as equilibrium is re-established.

concepts.name: Relating concentration changes
concepts.statement: Whatever the initial composition, the changes in the concentrations of the species in an equilibrium are related by the reaction stoichiometry, so all of them can be written as multiples of one unknown, $x$.

concepts.name: Calculating K with an ICE table
concepts.statement: Collecting the initial concentrations, their changes and the equilibrium concentrations in an ICE table derives every equilibrium concentration from the data given, and substituting them into the $K$ expression gives the equilibrium constant.

concepts.name: Calculating a missing equilibrium concentration
concepts.statement: When the equilibrium constant and all but one equilibrium concentration are known, the $K$ expression can be rearranged and solved for the missing concentration.

concepts.name: Calculating equilibrium concentrations from initial concentrations
concepts.statement: Four steps find the equilibrium composition from initial concentrations and $K$: identify the direction of reaction, develop an ICE table, solve for the change (by the quadratic formula where needed, keeping the physically meaningful root), and confirm the result by recalculating $K$.

concepts.name: Small-change approximation
concepts.statement: When $K$ is small, the change in concentration may be much less than the initial concentration, so the initial concentration minus $x$ can be approximated by the initial concentration. The result must be checked, and the calculation repeated without the approximation if $x$ is not negligible.

concepts.name: Brønsted-Lowry acids and bases
concepts.statement: Brønsted and Lowry defined acids and bases in terms of the transfer of hydrogen ions: a compound that donates a proton is a Brønsted-Lowry acid, and a compound that accepts a proton is a Brønsted-Lowry base. An acid-base reaction is, thus, the transfer of a proton from a donor to an acceptor.

concepts.name: Conjugate acid-base pairs
concepts.statement: When an acid donates H<sup>+</sup>, the species that remains is its conjugate base, because it reacts as a proton acceptor in the reverse reaction; when a base accepts H<sup>+</sup>, it is converted to its conjugate acid. Every Brønsted-Lowry reaction therefore involves two conjugate pairs.

concepts.name: Writing acid and base ionization equations
concepts.statement: Acid ionization is the reaction of an acid with water to give hydronium ion and the acid’s conjugate base; base ionization is the reaction of a base with water to give hydroxide ion and the base’s conjugate acid. Writing these equations requires identifying which species donates and which accepts the proton.

concepts.name: Amphiprotic species
concepts.statement: A species that can either donate or accept a proton is amphiprotic. Add one to water and it sets up both its acid and its base equilibria at the same time.

concepts.name: Autoionization of water
concepts.statement: Liquid water undergoes autoionization to a very slight extent, and the equilibrium constant for this reaction is the ion-product constant for water, $K_{\text{w}}$. The process is endothermic, so the extent of ionization, and with it $K_{\text{w}}$, increases with temperature.

concepts.name: Calculating ion concentrations in water
concepts.statement: Because the product of the hydronium and hydroxide ion concentrations is fixed by $K_{\text{w}}$, the two are inversely proportional: knowing one gives the other, and in pure water each is the square root of $K_{\text{w}}$.

concepts.name: Brønsted-Lowry acid
concepts.statement: A Brønsted-Lowry acid is a compound that donates a proton (H<sup>+</sup>) to another compound.

concepts.name: Brønsted-Lowry base
concepts.statement: A Brønsted-Lowry base is a compound that accepts a proton (H<sup>+</sup>) from another compound.

concepts.name: Conjugate acid
concepts.statement: The conjugate acid of a base is the species formed when the base accepts a proton.

concepts.name: Conjugate base
concepts.statement: The conjugate base of an acid is the species formed when the acid donates a proton.

concepts.name: Acid ionization
concepts.statement: Acid ionization is the reaction of an acid with water, yielding hydronium ion and the conjugate base of the acid.

concepts.name: Base ionization
concepts.statement: Base ionization is the reaction of a base with water, yielding hydroxide ion and the conjugate acid of the base.

concepts.name: Amphoteric
concepts.statement: An amphoteric species is one that can act as either an acid or a base.

concepts.name: Autoionization
concepts.statement: Autoionization is a reaction between identical species that yields ionic products; for water, two molecules react to give a hydronium ion and a hydroxide ion.

concepts.name: Ion-product constant for water
concepts.statement: The ion-product constant for water, $K_{\text{w}}$, is the equilibrium constant for the autoionization of water, the product of the hydronium and hydroxide ion concentrations; it is 1.0 × 10<sup>−14</sup> at 25 °C.

forms.condition: any aqueous solution at 25 °C

concepts.name: Acidic, basic, and neutral solutions
concepts.statement: A solution is neutral if it contains equal concentrations of hydronium and hydroxide ions, acidic if it contains a greater concentration of hydronium ions than hydroxide ions, and basic if it contains a lesser one. Since $K_{\text{w}}$ depends on temperature, the pH of a neutral solution does too.

concepts.name: pH and pOH scales
concepts.statement: Hydronium and hydroxide ion concentrations span many orders of magnitude, so they are expressed with the p-function, the negative base-10 logarithm: pH = −log[H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>] and pOH = −log[OH<sup>−</sup>]. Each unit of pH is a tenfold change in hydronium ion concentration.

concepts.name: Sum of pH and pOH
concepts.statement: Taking the negative logarithm of the $K_{\text{w}}$ expression shows that the pH and pOH of any aqueous solution sum to p$K_{\text{w}}$, which is 14.00 at 25 °C.

forms.condition: any aqueous solution at 25 °C

concepts.name: Converting between concentration, pH and pOH
concepts.statement: The definitions of pH and pOH and their sum let us move among [H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>], [OH<sup>−</sup>], pH, and pOH; when taking the log of a value, we keep as many decimal places in the result as there are significant figures in the value.

concepts.name: Measuring pH with meters and indicators
concepts.statement: The acidity of a solution is typically assessed by measuring its pH, directly with a pH meter or visually with colored indicators; the pOH is not usually measured, as it is easily calculated from the pH.

concepts.name: Acidic solution
concepts.statement: An acidic solution contains a greater concentration of hydronium ions than hydroxide ions.

concepts.name: Basic solution
concepts.statement: A basic solution contains a lesser concentration of hydronium ions than hydroxide ions.

concepts.name: Neutral solution
concepts.statement: A neutral solution contains equal concentrations of hydronium and hydroxide ions.

concepts.name: pH
concepts.statement: The pH of a solution is the negative base-10 logarithm of its hydronium ion molarity.

forms.condition: any aqueous solution
any aqueous solution

concepts.name: pOH
concepts.statement: The pOH of a solution is the negative base-10 logarithm of its hydroxide ion molarity.

forms.condition: any aqueous solution
any aqueous solution

concepts.name: Acid and base ionization constants
concepts.statement: The relative strength of an acid or base is the extent to which it ionizes in water, and it is quantified by the equilibrium constant of its ionization, $K_{\text{a}}$ or $K_{\text{b}}$, in which water, being the solvent, does not appear. The larger the constant, the stronger the acid or base.

concepts.name: Percent ionization
concepts.statement: Another measure of the strength of an acid is its percent ionization, the equilibrium hydronium ion concentration divided by the initial acid concentration, times 100. Unlike $K_{\text{a}}$, the percent ionization of a weak acid varies with its initial concentration, decreasing as the concentration increases.

forms.condition: a weak acid HA

concepts.name: Conjugate pair strengths
concepts.statement: Adding the acid ionization of HA to the base ionization of A<sup>−</sup> gives the autoionization of water, so the product of their constants is $K_{\text{w}}$. The stronger an acid or base, the weaker its conjugate partner, and the conjugate of a strong acid or base has negligible strength.

forms.condition: a conjugate acid-base pair at 25 °C

concepts.name: Leveling effect
concepts.statement: Acids stronger than H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> react completely with water to give H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>, and bases stronger than OH<sup>−</sup> react completely to give OH<sup>−</sup>, so in water all such acids and bases appear equally strong. Their differences show up only in a solvent that is a weaker base or acid than water.

concepts.name: Determining Ka or Kb
concepts.statement: Substituting equilibrium concentrations into the ionization constant expression gives $K_{\text{a}}$ or $K_{\text{b}}$ directly; when only the formal concentration and the pH are known, the pH gives the equilibrium [H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>] and an ICE table gives the rest.

concepts.name: Calculating weak acid or base equilibria
concepts.statement: An ICE table built from the initial concentration and the ionization constant gives the equilibrium concentrations. When the constant is small and the initial concentration large, the change $x$ may be neglected against it, provided $x$ is less than 5% of the initial concentration; otherwise the quadratic equation is solved.

concepts.name: Binary acid strength
concepts.statement: Across a row of the periodic table, the acid strength of binary hydrogen compounds increases with the electronegativity of the nonmetal, because the polarity of the H–A bond increases; down a group, it increases as the H–A bond strength decreases.

concepts.name: Strengths of oxyacids and hydroxy compounds
concepts.statement: In a ternary compound E–O–H, a central atom of low electronegativity makes the E–O bond ionic and the compound a base; a central atom of high electronegativity or high oxidation number draws electron density from the O–H bond and makes the compound an acid. Elements of intermediate electronegativity give amphoteric hydroxides.

concepts.name: Acid ionization constant
concepts.statement: The acid ionization constant, $K_{\text{a}}$, is the equilibrium constant for the ionization of a weak acid; its negative logarithm is p$K_{\text{a}}$.

forms.condition: the ionization HA + H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + A⁻ at equilibrium
any weak acid

concepts.name: Base ionization constant
concepts.statement: The base ionization constant, $K_{\text{b}}$, is the equilibrium constant for the ionization of a weak base; its negative logarithm is p$K_{\text{b}}$.

forms.condition: the ionization B + H₂O ⇌ HB⁺ + OH⁻ at equilibrium
any weak base

concepts.name: Acidic and basic ions in salts
concepts.statement: The ions of a dissolved salt may undergo acid or base ionization with water. Acidic cations are typically the conjugate acids of weak bases, basic anions are the conjugate bases of weak acids, and the conjugates of strong acids and bases, like the group 1 and 2 cations, are inert.

concepts.name: Predicting the acidity of a salt solution
concepts.statement: We consider each ion separately; where a salt contains both an acidic and a basic ion, or a single amphiprotic ion, the solution is acidic or basic according to whether $K_{\text{a}}$ or $K_{\text{b}}$ is the larger.

concepts.name: Calculating the pH of a salt solution
concepts.statement: The ionization constant of a salt’s acidic or basic ion is found from that of its conjugate partner through $K_{\text{a}}\times K_{\text{b}}=K_{\text{w}}$, and the usual ICE approach then gives the equilibrium concentrations and the pH.

concepts.name: Hydrated metal ions as acids
concepts.statement: Many metal ions bond to water molecules to form complex ions such as [Al(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup>; the metal draws electron density from the bonded water molecules, weakening their O–H bonds so that they can donate protons. Aside from the group 1 and some group 2 ions, most metal ions undergo acid ionization to some extent.

concepts.name: Polyprotic acids ionize stepwise
concepts.statement: Acids are classified by the number of protons per molecule they can give up: monoprotic, diprotic, triprotic. A polyprotic acid ionizes in steps, one proton at a time, and each successive ionization is less extensive than the one before, so $K_{\text{a1}}>K_{\text{a2}}>K_{\text{a3}}$.

concepts.name: Calculating polyprotic acid concentrations
concepts.statement: If the first ionization constant of a weak diprotic acid is larger than the second by a factor of at least 20, each step may be treated separately: the first gives [H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>] and the monoanion, and those concentrations feed the second.

concepts.name: Polyprotic bases
concepts.statement: Polyprotic bases accept more than one proton, in steps, and, as for polyprotic acids, each successive base ionization constant is smaller than the one before.

concepts.name: Monoprotic acid
concepts.statement: A monoprotic acid is an acid containing one ionizable hydrogen atom per molecule.

concepts.name: Diprotic acid
concepts.statement: A diprotic acid is an acid containing two ionizable hydrogen atoms per molecule.

concepts.name: Triprotic acid
concepts.statement: A triprotic acid is an acid that contains three ionizable hydrogen atoms per molecule.

concepts.name: Diprotic base
concepts.statement: A diprotic base is a base capable of accepting two protons.

concepts.name: Stepwise ionization
concepts.statement: Stepwise ionization is the process in which an acid is ionized by losing protons sequentially, one at a time.

concepts.name: What a buffer is
concepts.statement: A solution containing appreciable amounts of a weak conjugate acid-base pair is a buffer, and it resists a change in pH when small amounts of a strong acid or a strong base are added.

concepts.name: How buffers work
concepts.statement: The weak acid of the pair neutralizes added hydroxide, converting it to the conjugate base, and the conjugate base neutralizes added hydronium, converting it to the weak acid. The ratio of the two changes only a little, and so does the pH.

concepts.name: Calculating buffer pH
concepts.statement: We first let the added strong acid or base react completely with the buffer component that neutralizes it, find the new concentrations of the two components, and then solve the equilibrium as before.

concepts.name: Buffer capacity
concepts.statement: The buffer capacity is the amount of acid or base that can be added to a given volume of a buffer before its pH changes significantly.
